author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

title: Khartoum courts UN-backed relief to stave off truce pressure; Tasis govt heedful after health minister’s angry exit; Abyei strike tests Juba ties; Drones hit RSF, military’s seats of power; RSF pushes in Kurmuk, military wins Geisan ground
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter


here

.


From Khartoum and Nyala, to a gold mine in South Kordofan, a town in West Kordofan and a power station in White Nile, drones tore through Sudan this week, killing hundreds and destroying homes, livelihoods and critical infrastructure.


Both sides traded blame, and each pointed to neighbors it said let the drones through. Some strikes went unclaimed, but silence from the military over its attack on the disputed Abyei region didn’t stop Juba from summoning Sudan’s ambassador on the same day to warn of a “dangerous development” in a border territory already straining relations between the two countries. Khartoum weighed in days later, with a Foreign Ministry statement denying the military was involved.


The strike on the RSF-held Naam market in Abyei set fuel depots burning. The fires were still consuming the area as the death toll exceeded 150 and thousands were displaced, and residents took to the streets in protest, activists and Abyei administration sources said.


In the Security Council, in Geneva and among mediators on Sudan, the warnings this week over the drone war and the humanitarian toll sounded much as they have for months, and they still amount to little beyond adding pressure on the warring parties to stop the fighting.


But Khartoum won’t concede an end to

RSF territorial control

before a truce can take hold, and won’t see the paramilitary group at the table in any political process on the country’s future.


So instead of committing to a broader settlement, it is now trying to show it can deliver on humanitarian issues, betting that progress on aid deliveries and civilian protection will

blunt

 international criticism, former and current Sudanese officials and sources close to the Transitional Sovereignty Council told Mada Masr.


Hence the letters to Western capitals over the week and the talks with the United Nations on internationally monitored aid deliveries, which allow Khartoum to appear willing to engage without participating on terms it rejects, former officials said. Any plan, however, has to keep aid under the authority of state institutions, they added.


In western Sudan, the RSF’s parallel administration is trying to hold on to the very recognition Khartoum is trying to deny it, but its own infighting is getting in the way. Tasis’s Cabinet is trying to take oversight of medical aid away from a health minister who had protested for months over interference by the RSF and influential figures looking to monopolize medical supplies. He left for Nairobi in protest last week, and a government already reeling from recent defections is treading carefully, wary of another exit that would further damage its image as a viable administration before aid organizations.


In Blue Nile State, the push and pull on the battlefield goes on. The RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, tried to take two of the military’s bases in Kurmuk locality, part of the network protecting the state capital of Damazin, though accounts of how it ended conflict. The military, meanwhile, gained ground in neighboring Geisan locality, taking two areas that a former military officer said could help check the RSF’s new advances in Wad al-Mahi locality.


***


Military drone strike on Abyei market draws protest from Juba


Caption: Undersecretary of the South Sudanese Foreign Ministry Agnes Adlino Orifa Oswaha and Sudan’s ambassador to Juba, Essam Karar, discuss the attack on the Naam market in Abyei, October 19. Courtesy: The South Sudanese Foreign Ministry via Facebook.


A drone strike carried out by the military on the Naam market in northern Abyei — the disputed border territory between South Sudan and Sudan’s RSF-held West Kordofan — on Monday has stoked new diplomatic friction between Khartoum and Juba.


The death toll from the strike has risen to more than 150, as efforts to recover bodies were initially hampered by fires spreading from fuel depots hit in the attack, a South Sudanese source in the office of

Yohana Akol Ngor

, the caretaker information minister in the Abyei administration, told Mada Masr.

 Around 8,000 people have also been displaced, the source said.


Juba responded by

summoning

Sudan’s ambassador to Juba,

Essam Karar

, on the same day to protest the attack, a source at the South Sudanese Foreign Ministry told Mada Masr.

author: Karyn Pugliese | Keelan Jacobs
title: Diplomats and disrupters: First Nations get set for a meeting with Canada’s leaders with ceremony
content:
On Sunday, chiefs set up teepees on the lawn behind 111 Sussex Drive, Ottawa’s old city hall which is now owned by the federal government.


They lit a sacred fire and gathered in a circle around it, some in chairs pulled out onto the grass, some stood, through prayers and a pipe ceremony, then a water ceremony.


” You know, don’t be afraid to ask for a miracle, and that’s what I’m praying here for, for miracles to happen at the meeting tomorrow,” said Piikani Elder Leonard Weasel Traveller, who emceed part of the Sunday events.


The morning belonged to First Nations. At noon, several premiers arrived, along with some federal ministers. Other provinces sent representatives. Each leader, First Nation and non-First Nation, was handed a red tobacco tie and asked to place it on the land.


Piikani Elder Leonard Weasel Traveller at the ceremony in Ottawa. Photo: Karyn Pugliese/APTN.


“I offer you this tobacco. It’s my offering today. Accept my prayer request. I ask you to, to help our chiefs, our leaders, to empower them with their message to the prime minister, their me- with their message to the premiers, so that we can have an opportunity to move forward with the challenges, the respective challenges that we have within all our First Nations,” said Weasel Traveller.


Then Assembly of First Nations (AFN) National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak led the group to a tree at the far end of the field beside the teepees, where one by one they placed their ties.


Woodhouse Nepinak said the ceremonies were needed to get all leaders into the right mindset and help the meeting unfold in a good way.


“ Instead of us always being in the courtroom, we should be in political rooms like this, talking with each other. Our chiefs should be given and First Nations should be given that respect, as well as the provinces and federal government. And things aren’t always gonna be easy.


“Conversations between each other have not always been easy,” said Woodhouse Nepinak.


“ I want to share that ceremony that is considered very essential to establish and building important relationships and to conduct dialogue in a good way. Ceremony is an expression of purpose and intent. It calls on each of us to orient our hearts, our minds and spirits in a positive way.”But what is a good way? That’s always been the question.


Do you knock on Ottawa’s door, or do you kick it in?


Inside Ottawa’s old city hall just a kilometre or so from Parliament Hill, regional chiefs of the AFN and a handful of chiefs selected to represent their regions will sit down with the Prime Minister Mark Carney and the premiers.


Outside, Onion Lake Cree Nation and a handful of activists plan to join a national day of action to decry the meeting. They’re worried about the erosion of treaty rights to land and water.


Some of the chiefs inside share those concerns.


No agenda has been shared publicly, but Chief Rodger Redman of Standing Buffalo Dakota Nation said he will have three minutes to speak.


He plans to use them on to talk about the climate, the environment and UNDRIP.


His list of concerns includes small modular reactors in Saskatchewan, which he expects will open up more uranium mining in the province’s north. Data centres. Relations with the EU. All without consultation, he said.


“ They’re selling, they’re selling Mother Earth. They’re pimping out Mother Earth to all these countries across, and we’re saying we need to stand up and protect the environment, Mother Earth, and everything that has that living spirit,” said Redman.


Bell’s AI data centre project near Regina carries an estimated price tag of $52 billion. An Angus Reid poll released this month found 70 per cent of Saskatchewan residents want data centre development in the province limited.


Redman said no one has done the due diligence on what it will mean for First Nations people, their water, their land and their inherent rights.


His nation reached out to the province. No response. To the Privy Council Office. No response. To industry, including Bell. Bell answered, but said it could only share that information with regulators.


‘ They’re selling, they’re selling Mother Earth. They’re pimping out Mother Earth to all these countries… says Redman. Photo: Karyn Pugliese/APTN.


“We have to put those hidden agendas on the table for First Nations,” he told reporters, and that’s what he plans to say in his allotted three minutes tomorrow.


However, the public will not hear those remarks.

title: Israel Launches Major Ethnic Cleansing Escalation in West Bank, Targeting Hebron
content:
The operation follows a Palestinian resistance attack on an illegal West Bank military checkpoint.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Israeli forces on Friday began demolishing homes and businesses and forcibly evacuating residents near Hebron in the illegally occupied West Bank following a Palestinian resistance attack that killed two Israeli soldiers.

“First, we will destroy this place and completely transform it, but we will do something that has never been done before,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said at the scene of the shooting attack that took place earlier Friday near Hebron Junction. “We will evacuate the residents, go from house to house, remove weapons from there as well, and deal with and destroy all terrorist infrastructure.”

“We will consider expanding this model to other cities as well,” Netanyahu added.

As expected, Israel kills Palestinians every day for months on end and nobody bats an eye; Palestinians finally respond, attacking Israeli soldiers at an Israeli military checkpoint on occupied Palestinian land, and its front page news and Israel makes the entire West Bank pay. https://t.co/iaSYIE7AML

The prime minister also ordered the Israeli military to “immediately impose a lockdown on Hebron and prepare for a full lockdown” of the entire West Bank, while vowing to launch the largest military operation in the occupied territory since it was conquered during the 1967 Six-Day War and subsequently ethnically cleansed of more than 100,000 Palestinians.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz also vowed that neighborhoods associated with the attackers would be “evacuated” — a word that critics call a euphemism for ethnic cleansing — “just like in Gaza; just like in Lebanon.”

Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich echoed those calls.

“There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign in Judea and Samaria to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons, and eliminate terrorists,” he said, referring to Israel’s name for the West Bank.

“Exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon,” Smotrich added.

Israeli occupation forces are forcibly evacuating residents from their homes in preparation for demolishing them in the Farsh al-Hawa area of Hebron. pic.twitter.com/KaDpsbVFNc

Israeli forces have killed or wounded more than 250,000 people in Gaza since the Hamas-led attack of October 2023, while forcibly displacing around 1.9 million residents and destroying or damaging more than 80% of the strip’s structures. In Lebanon, nearly 40,000 people have been killed or injured by Israeli attacks over the same period, during which there were two waves of mass displacement in which more than a million people were forced from their homes each time. Dozens of Lebanese villages have been flattened.

Demolition and displacement were the order of the day in the West Bank Friday as Israeli bulldozers began demolishing homes after Netanyahu’s announcement, even as local residents said their properties had no connection to the attack on the slain Israeli troops.

The Times of Israel reported that soldiers ordered Palestinians in the Farsh al-Hawa area to evacuate ahead of demolitions, with footage showing residents being pushed out as their belongings were loaded onto trucks.

“We are already here with the equipment on the ground, sending an unequivocal message to our enemies: If you mess with us, we will exact a very, very painful price from you,” Smotrich said in Farsh al-Hawa.

Israeli occupation forces begin a large-scale demolition operation near the site of a shooting attack that killed two Israeli soldiers and injured others in the Farsh al-Hawa area of Hebron. pic.twitter.com/H5DEHvMKbr

Israel’s High Court intervened and issued a temporary order to halt demolitions after Arab-Israeli human rights lawyer Mohammed Dahleh filed an urgent petition on behalf of two factory owners who claimed the destruction violated Israeli law as well as international prohibitions on collective punishment.

“What we saw today was an attempt to copy the illegal practices used in Gaza, in the heart of the West Bank,” Dahleh told The Guardian. “They want to wipe out entire areas exactly as they did in Gaza and the refugee camps in the West Bank.”

Another Israeli human rights attorney, Michael Sfard, called Smotrich’s video announcement a “direct admission” of collective punishment …

author: Randi Beers
title: Jimmy Bell – An Arctic trader
content:
Young Jimmy Bell stood 5’10” tall and weighed about 170 pounds when he joined the Hudson’s Bay Co. as a 19-year-old recruit in 1925.


Two decades later his weight had more than doubled, by some reports reaching 350 pounds. The Inuit, whom he knew and loved, and who knew and loved him, called him Quinijuq – the fat man.


Bell was born in Cromdale, Scotland, the eldest son in a large family. He walked three miles to school and back each day during eight years of primary school and followed that with three years of higher education.


Then Bell worked as a bookkeeper for a local garage for three years until he emigrated to Canada as a young fur trader, following in the footsteps of so many young Scots before him. 


Montreal, the city where he first set foot in Canada, was always dear to him. Much later, he decided that he would eventually retire there, but it was never to be.


That summer of 1925 he travelled on the Hudson’s Bay Company supply ship to Lake Harbour (now Kimmirut) where he was apprentice clerk for three years, before moving on to Frobisher Bay for two years in the same position.


After a year’s furlough, Bell was posted for one year as manager at Payne Bay in northern Quebec, a post he described as the poorest-looking he had seen. He followed that with two years each again in Frobisher Bay and Lake Harbour. 


After another year of furlough, Bell returned to Lake Harbour for another five years, before spending short periods at the Winnipeg Depot and Cross Lake, Man. Then he spent four years, from 1942 to 1946, as manager in Arctic Bay.


After a short holiday, Bell returned for a fourth tour of duty at Lake Harbour, only a year this time, before transferring to Cape Dorset for his final year in the Arctic and his final year of life.


Bell loved Arctic Bay, the company’s most northerly post. He was a sociable man, a good cook and a gracious host. Visitors were always welcome, whether they be other traders, missionaries, policemen, or Inuit. He liked to eat, drink, play bridge, and tell stories.


Yet one sketch of his life says, “Those he liked thought he was wonderful. Those who didn’t found him dour and reserved.”


Bell had an enormous appetite and it was said that he could eat eight to 10 pounds of seal meat at one sitting. There was a Department of Transport weather station in Arctic Bay and Bell got in the habit of visiting for Sunday supper, bringing “his huge bulk and fund of stories.”


All post managers were required to keep a daily journal and a monthly summary of their journals. For some, it was a sparse record of the comings and goings of the Inuit to the post to trade, usually with remarks on the weather. But Bell’s journals were more than that.


Rather than just a bare record of trading activities, he took time to write in detail about the visits of the Inuit and observances of nature. They were carefully written and showed a love of language.


In May of 1944 he wrote, “The first snow-birds of the season were observed on the 10

th

, which is almost three weeks later than their first appearance last year. These hardy little birds must still find the Arctic nights rather chilly.” 


Bell showed the same care when writing about the Inuit.


That same month, when Tonga died at Cape Cunningham, he wrote, “He was the oldest native in the territory and we believe the last of the ‘Angakoks’… [H]e was the last strong link with paganism. We think, however, that the old man’s brand of pagan religion was just as good as that taught by the Missionaries; at least Tonga was less deceitful than some of his brethren who have seen the ‘light.’”  


Such detail in a journal is all the more remarkable when one realizes that probably no one other than his district manager in Winnipeg would read his words at the time. 


Bell’s Hudson’s Bay Company service record describes him as a “good reliable type,” and a “first class Eskimo trader.” One report called him a “permanent Arctic man,” but noted ominously that he was “dangerously obese.” 


Bell loved his drink. He spent Christmas Day 1933 at Frobisher Bay working, and wrote, “Christmas Day was spent in the store, where 83 foxes were traded. At night I celebrated Xmas by having a fire in the guardroom [sitting room] and having a better meal than usual. I also put up with the torture of a collar and tie, and toasted the health of absent friends in lime juice; not that it was necessary to do so, as I have three kinds of strong drink on the post, but there …

author: By John Malamatinas, Contributor
title: TikTok Revolt in France: A New Generation Takes To The Streets
content:
On October 17, France witnessed some of the most intense urban unrest in its recent history. Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across the country, while clashes with police, widespread looting, and burning barricades transformed the streets of numerous cities. Activists described the events to Unicorn Riot as among “the fiercest riots France has experienced since World War II.”


The protests were not confined to Paris. From Marseille and Lyon to Bordeaux, Limoges, and numerous smaller cities, demonstrators confronted police, occupied streets, and attacked commercial and government buildings.


The mobilization had begun weeks earlier. On September 7, a young TikToker called for a revival of the Yellow Vests movement, which had shaken France in 2018 and 2019. The immediate trigger of the original movement was the rising price of fuel, which had climbed above two euros per liter.


Meanwhile, an independent wave of high school protests was spreading across France. Students were protesting deteriorating school infrastructure, chronic underfunding of public education, and worsening conditions in classrooms. Hundreds of schools were reportedly occupied or blockaded during the preceding weeks.


These two mobilizations began to reinforce each other, turning October 17 into a focal point for broader social discontent. On TikTok, a veritable media storm unfolded. AI-generated videos, influencers, humorous memes, and countless short clips promoted the demonstrations and in the prospect of a Yellow Vests comeback. Old footage from the movement was recreated, remixed, and circulated to a new generation. High school students were particularly active. In videos shared across social media, groups of students danced to the viral song “Hey Mr. Policeman” in front of police lines during their demonstrations. By Saturday, the mobilization had reached an extraordinary scale.


According to organizers, approximately 800,000 people demonstrated across France. The Interior Ministry estimated 550,000 participants, including 110,000 in Paris. For comparison, during the massive mobilization against the Loi Travail labor reforms on June 14, 2016, organizers estimated that 1.3 million people had taken to the streets nationwide.


The protests developed into widespread urban unrest with

more than 2,000 businesses

 attacked or looted, vehicles set on fire, and government buildings targeted. In Limoges, masked individuals entered the historic 19th-century city hall and set it ablaze. The fire destroyed large parts of the building, including its roof. In Marseille, protesters forced their way into city hall.


“Stop shooting out the eyes of high school students and ordinary people. These are people who are studying. And you’re blinding people, you’re blinding people who are studying. These are people, they’re victims, and you’re hurting them.”


Paris: The Streets Breakaway From the Official March


The morning in Paris began with relatively unsuccessful attempts to mobilize around several railway stations. Groups of protesters were repeatedly surrounded or dispersed by police, preventing them from gathering in larger numbers.


By approximately 2 p.m., however, the center of the mobilization had shifted to Place de la République, where tens of thousands of people assembled. 


As the first confrontations with police began, protesters gathered around the monumental statue of Marianne, the symbolic representation of the French Republic. Activists had dressed the statue in an enormous yellow vest. One side carried a message referring to October 17, 1961, when Paris police massacred Algerian demonstrators protesting a discriminatory curfew. The other side denounced the treatment of students by police in 2026.


The symbolism was unmistakable: the current revolt was being connected to France’s history of colonial violence and contemporary police repression.


What followed was difficult to describe: rather than following the conventional and thus predetermined demonstration route, large groups of protesters began moving in multiple directions.


Traditionally, major demonstrations in Paris follow routes negotiated between unions and authorities, often connecting large squares such as République, Bastille, or Nation. These routes allow police to concentrate their forces and contain demonstrations within relatively predictable boundaries. On October 17, that model collapsed.

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Making Women’s History Part of the Curriculum
content:
Two teachers from Sacred Heart Preparatory School in California, Kristen Kelly and Serene Williams, have proposed an Advanced Placement U.S. Women’s History course in response to the issue of students not learning about women’s history. The courses would allow studying women’s experiences and contributions in greater depth. Establishing this course would create a better understanding of American history as it includes the diverse experiences of women and would help students connect the historical struggles for equality to gender issues today.

Women have contributed to shaping the nation’s politics, economy, and social movements, yet their participation is often overlooked by traditional history classes. From fighting for the right to vote, challenging discrimination, and advocating for female autonomy, women have had a significant role in building the foundation of the United States today.

One of the main arguments for WAPUSH is that women’s experiences are not explored in the classroom. In the article Educational Activism: Creating an AP U.S. Women’s History Course, Serene Williams, Kristen Kelly, and Clara Robinson explain that topics such as women’s suffrage and reproductive rights receive limited attention in the current AP U.S. History curriculum. The women’s suffrage movement involved decades of organizing, political campaigning, and resistance. However, teachers may not introduce this topic to students or have enough time to examine its strategies and leaders in detail. A dedicated course would allow students to study these movements more thoroughly and understand how women helped shape American democracy.

Women’s history is much broader than the fight for voting rights. The proposed WAPUSH curriculum includes women’s labor, politics, religion, culture, war, and violence against women. It also examines how race, class, sexuality, religion, and other identities shaped women’s experiences. This approach is important because women throughout the years have never shared one universal experience. Indigenous women, Black women, Immigrant women, etc., have faced different opportunities and forms of discrimination. Studying these differences would help students develop a greater understanding of American history and that America was not built on just our founding fathers, but by women who paved the path for opportunity and development through blood, sweat, and tears.

An AP course would also help students recognize the connection between historical events and current issues. The debate over reproductive rights and other feminist struggles today cannot be fully understood without examining the laws and political movements that shaped access to contraceptives, abortion, and female economic support. Studying topics from the suffrage movement to the Equal Rights Amendment can help students understand the political equality that has developed through activism and engage in feminist discussion. Learning this history would give students the context needed to evaluate debates instead of viewing them as different events.

Establishing this course would show that women’s history is worthy of advanced academic study. The WAPUSH campaign began in 2022, and according to its website, the campaign gathered more than 4,000 petition signatures and received encouragement from College Board leadership as it worked toward launching this course. Its proposal has also received university support, while the campaign continues seeking letters from high schools willing to offer the course. This continued support brings women closer to bringing light to women’s history and giving women a space in school systems and curricula. This petition is one step closer every day to its goal to educate and inform people all across America of women’s contributions.

An AP U.S. Women’s History course would make education more comprehensive, inform students even more about the history of the U.S., and connect past struggles to present issues. Women have influenced American politics, economics, culture, and social movements, yet their experiences are not always given sufficient attention in existing courses. By offering students an opportunity to examine these experiences, the College Board could help create a more inclusive and accurate understanding of the nation’s past. Women’s history is not separate from American history but instead an essential part of it.

author: Santana Dreaver
title: ‘Gratifying and humbling’: First Nation leads ghost net cleanup from Interior ‘B.C.’ rivers
content:
Volunteers Lyza Adoplh, John Redan, Nick Froese and Roxx Ledoux work to haul abandoned fishing gear out of the Fraser and Thompson rivers. Photo by Santana Dreaver


This article has been co-published

with the Narwhal

 as part of their

2026 Indigenous journalism fellowship

.


After starting the day with a prayer and a safety demonstration, a group of volunteers gears up in water-resistant clothing and lifejackets, ready to hit the water.


The crew is preparing to scour a stretch of the Fraser and Thompson rivers, removing any fishing gear or waste left behind. Fishing nets left underneath the water are commonly known as ghost nets, which trap and kill fish. 


As the saying goes on a volunteer call out poster, “ghost nets create ghost fish.”


TLKemchEEN (Lytton First Nation) has led the river clean-up program in the area for the past 20 years, all in an effort to preserve salmon populations and aquatic life following harvest season.


Over two days in September, a group of 40 volunteers spent a total of 20 combined hours on the water.


From Lillooet to Lytton during the first day, and from Lytton to Yale during the second day, volunteers passed through white-water rapids and rugged terrain such as the famously turbulent passage of Hell’s Gate.


When the raft leader yells “hold on,” that’s exactly what participants do, reaching down for a rope attached to the raft, laughing and hollering, ripping through the Fraser Canyon rapids. 


The cold river water splashes everyone — waking up the crew as countless bald and golden eagles watch from above.


“I didn’t realize how impactful everything is along the shores. I guess I didn’t realize that some leave their garbage and nets out there,” volunteer Rebecca Riley, who is from the Stʼatʼimc Nation, said.


“Once I saw that with my own eyes, I wanted to jump in and be a part of it.”


A newspaper ad about the river clean-up project inspired Rebecca Riley to get involved. She has helped remove ghost nets since 2018. Photo: Supplied by Rebecca Riley


‘That fishery is a communal right’


It’s a sentiment shared by many volunteers on the boat, who eagerly approach the shoreline when a ghost net comes into sight. 


Whether the net will take one person to remove, or up to five to pull out of the water, is unknown until people get their hands wet. 


During the non-rapid portion of the cleanup, countless stories were told, Indigenous people exchanged words in their languages to compare similarities and differences and folks even had hot chocolate along the shore, courtesy of Kumsheen Rafting, which was contracted to support the program this year. 


During the first year of the program, 126 ghost nets were collected.


“This year we picked up six nets and some garbage, some years prior we’ve picked up zero. We have to remind our fishermen not to be lazy and take their gear home,” Kevin Duncan told the Narwhal.


Duncan is an elected councillor for TLKemchEEN in “B.C.’s” Southern Interior, part of the Nlaka’pamux Nation Tribal Council. He has been involved with the program since its inception. He attended both cleanup days this year with his son, Aaron.


Kevin Duncan, an elected councillor for TLKemchEEN, has been involved in Lytton’s ghost net clean-up initiative since it started 20 years ago. He always leads a prayer before they begin. Photo: Supplied by Rebecca Riley


For TLKemchEEN, stewarding their waters as they always have is crucial — especially as salmon numbers decline. Life along the Fraser and Thompson rivers is deeply connected to salmon. And TLKemchEEn is home to where the two rivers meet, in the country’s largest salmon-bearing watershed.


“For future generations, sometime down the road, I’m afraid all they’re going to be looking at is pictures of salmon in a book,” said Duncan. 


The nets recovered by the program are given to those in need, including single mothers, low-income families and Elders from the nation. 


“As a Nlaka’pamux or Stʼatʼimc member … that fishery is a communal right, it’s not an individual right. It’s looked after by your nation,” Duncan said.


“Most times, you just get to see portions of the river from the highway, but once you’re down on the water, floating for eight hours from Lillooet to Lytton, it gives you a better perspective on where people fish.” 


Now 20 years into the program, volunteer spots fill up months in advance. Photo by Santana Dreaver


Removing fishing gear from the cold and fast-moving river can be …

author: Mehk Chakraborty
title: Inside the resistance to Spain’s crackdown on migrants in Ceuta
content:
This article

Inside the resistance to Spain’s crackdown on migrants in Ceuta

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


On July 30, images streamed across TVs, social media feeds and newspapers of thousands of people approaching a fence along the beach, in boats and by foot. Migrants, including children and families, were attempting to cross into Ceuta, a Spanish enclave bordered by Morocco. Facing violent border guards and the threat of drowning, over 70,000 people made it to Ceuta, with hopes of eventually reaching the Spanish mainland. Officials in Ceuta

said

 that 100 people died in the crossing — either by drowning or being crushed — and sources on the ground believe the number was higher. 


“I lost my phone, my money, my ID card, everything I had,” one Moroccan teenager recalled. “At one point I got pulled to the bottom, so far down that my feet touched the sand. When I looked around me, I saw women and babies who had drowned.”


“There was no proper humanitarian response from the local authorities — whether it is basic hygiene, food or shelter,” said Ric Fernández, coordinator and spokesperson for humanitarian and migrant advocacy group No Name Kitchen, or NNK, about the first days after the mass crossing. “Instead, there was an institutional response of pressuring people to ‘voluntarily’ return to Morocco. … There was repression, violence against people on the move in every form — legal, administrative and physical, and the forced expulsion of people.”   


Facing intense pressure and violence from both the Spanish police and military, within 96 hours most people returned to Morocco. Estimates about how many migrants remain are in flux, but the Spanish government

said

 in late September that up to 10,000 people are still in Ceuta.


While the global mainstream media quickly moved on from this story, the situation in Ceuta has

remained tense

 over the last three months, with increased violent harassment by the police, evictions and collective expulsions. In recent weeks,

“voluntary returns” and evictions

 from makeshift camps on the beach have ramped up.


Embed from Getty Images


Irene Estébanez Gutiérrez, a family and community doctor in Madrid, spent two weeks in Ceuta as a volunteer. “An information campaign has been waged that portrays people on the move as invaders, violent and dangerous,” she said. The

media coverage

, she believes, has failed to adequately address “the resulting humanitarian crisis, the systematic violation of rights, the lack of protection for minors, and the systematic violence and discrimination to which people are being subjected to, particularly by the military.”


Those who remain include Moroccan men and women, alongside Sudanese, Syrians, Palestinians, Malians and Nigerians. According to NNK, a significant number are minors. They are still stranded; the majority of them have slept in the street or in makeshift tents since they crossed into Ceuta over two months ago. 


Kora, who uses a pseudonym as an activist to protect her identity, arrived in Ceuta to volunteer in early August and found the violence and the lack of access to basic necessities particularly angering. The authorities were “not letting them access the supermarkets to get food or water,” she said. “They turned off the publicly and freely accessible water [to shower or drink] on the beaches and beat them or scare them in the middle of the night … to purposefully making their lives more miserable.” 


Organizing solidarity, facing criminalization


This

violence

, however, did not prevent activists and migrants from developing forms of organizing and resistance. Hundreds of migrants

staged a protest

 on a popular beach in Ceuta in August to demand asylum. On Sept. 21, Migreurop, a Euro-African network of organizations, activists and researchers that monitors European migration policies, noted in a

joint statement

 with over 100 organizations: “We have witnessed forms of resistance in everyday survival practices.” They mentioned the sharing of information, food and medicine, as well as safety and protection practices.

We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Besides migrants’ self-led efforts, civil society has stepped up to help, with the Spanish Red Cross

distributing food

 at Trampolín Beach, the site of one makeshift camp. Other local charities like Luna Blanca, have been

providing

author: C4SS
title: C4SS Panelists on the Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie
content:
The

Markets and Society conference

 this weekend (October 23-26) will feature many interesting panels on topics from public policy to self-governance to digital privacy to immigration and beyond. There will also be longtime C4SSers presenting.


On

Saturday from 9:00-10:30am

, Nathan Goodman is chairing the panel “The Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie” featuring:


Cory Massimino – National Economic Planning: What is Right?


Don Lavoie argued in “National Economic Planning: What is Left?” that economic planning was inherently reactionary and thwarted genuinely left-wing aims like peace and liberation. Despite the prevailing conservative-libertarian fusionism of Lavoie’s day, his study of economics and history helped him see the transience of such an alliance: libertarianism was left-wing until the left became obsessed with economic planning and the right was always about militarism and hierarchy no matter how much libertarian rhetoric it adopted. Lavoie’s new (yet old) framing went under appreciated during his time and deserves careful reconsidering for anticipating the contemporary right’s increasing authoritarianism. This essay will build on Lavoie’s framing of economic planning as essentially right-wing, apply that framing to the contemporary American political situation, and argue such a framing is essential for any coherent conception of the political landscape going forward.


Jason Lee Byas – A Role For Lavoian Democracy


Don Lavoie argues for detaching our concept of democracy from the particular institution of voting, and instead seeing it as “openness,” or accessible means to shaping the world around you and its rules. An advantage of this approach is its complementarity with markets and property rights, which might otherwise be seen as in tension with democracy — thus partially reuniting liberalism’s “libertarian” and “democratic” commitments. Yet there is still a tension here. Philosophically, many libertarians may think that any social rules involving force should simply be set by natural rights, and so leaving these open to adjustment by anyone at all (let alone with open access to everyone) will be a problem. Practically, open access to reshaping the rules may spell uncertainty in problematic ways. I resolve these remaining tensions by suggesting a specific role for Lavoian Democracy. In short, many things are left radically indeterminate by any socially-practiced system of rights, and so too are many things left radically indeterminate by a commitment to natural rights. Questions of interpretation and resolution loom large, and the process of interpretation and resolution can either be hierarchical and authoritarian, or a product of ground-up contestation. There are principled liberal grounds — both moral and epistemic — for favoring the latter, and this is the role for Lavoian Democracy. I then offer a handful of institutions and practices that Lavoian Democracy might favor, including unions (of a certain form), adverse possession, and the common law.


Akiva Malamet – Beyond Recognition: Identity, Cultural Discovery, and the Limits of Social Planning


Scholars in liberal theory and political economy have long emphasized what Don Lavoie called the “knowledge problem”: social information is dispersed, local, emergent, and personal, and thus inaccessible to centralized or “high modernist” institutions. Lavoie and others showed that state economic planning fails because planners cannot access or generate this kind of knowledge and often undermine its creation. Liberal institutions, by contrast, enable people to align diverse plans and generate forms of knowledge no top-down authority could anticipate. I extend these insights to issues of identity, cultural development, and interpersonal life. Identity and cultural formation are bottom-up, organic processes reflecting the nuances of how people self-conceive, relate, and find meaning. State planning and institutional treatments of identity often obstruct pluralistic self-concepts and cultural discovery, flattening human diversity and complex individual lives into simple, legible categories. Ironically, formal recognition can perpetuate the injustices it was intended to remedy and reinforce intergroup conflict. State recognition of identity undermines the processes through which identity becomes meaningful, and conflicts with core liberal values of pluralism, self-authorship, and cooperation. Immigration restrictions present an analogous case: they …

title: Introducing the NSPM-7 Defendants Union
content:
Earlier this month,

The Guardian


announced

 the existence of the

NSPM-7 Defendants Union

, a new experiment in movement defense. We reached out to the organizers for an overview of their project, which we present here.


Announcing the NSPM-7 Defendants Union


National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (NSPM-7) is a government-wide strategy to investigate, disrupt, and prosecute what the Trump administration calls “left-wing political extremism.” They have already used it to justify publicly killing Minneapolis anti-ICE rapid responders Renee Good and Alex Pretti,

raiding the homes

 of University of Michigan students protesting the genocide of Palestinians, and

re-indicting

 Stop Cop City protesters.


But by the tens of thousands, newly politicized people are learning to fight: Minnesotan moms tracking BORTAC agents, students throwing back tear gas outside

Delaney Hall

, nurses making split-decisions to help people escape from ICE. Especially in the movement against Trump’s deportation agenda, thousands of people are taking brave actions for the first time.


NSPM-7 is intended to turn their lives upside down. We want to make them stronger.


For decades, social movements have developed strategies to withstand repression, learn, and propagate revolutionary politics. Those of us who have had our homes raided, organized collective defense,

resisted grand juries

, built

support committees

, devised

media strategies

, and stayed active through periods of repression have something valuable to offer the growing list of NSPM-7 defendants. That’s why we built the NSPM-7 Defendants Union.


We aim to make our social movements resilient. To do so, we need to make everyone aware of Trump’s strategy to crush dissent and mount a common defense against it while recentering the discussion about what Trump calls “antifa” on our own terms, so that we can speak proudly and publicly in defense of our politics and our resistance.


The Defendants Pledge


NSPM-7 treats Trump’s adversaries as if they all comprise a single united movement. We should use that to our advantage. We want a critical mass of new defendants across the country to adopt a shared framework to fight their cases. If everyone embraces bold, political publicity and commits to collective defense, we could amass leverage across hundreds of cases.


We want you to take this

pledge

 if you are a political defendant, if you have been contacted by the police or federal agents, if you are under surveillance, or if you believe that any of these things could happen in the foreseeable future. We take this pledge across movements, as a promise to each other.


I pledge:


To Go Public with My Case

: I will not be quiet. I want as large an audience as possible to know about my case.


To Benefit the Movement

: When I talk about my case, I will link it to the larger movement. I will use the platform of my case to spread the ideas and values of the movement, so that many more people can learn what I believe in and be inspired by those ideas as well.


To Share Lessons Learned

: I will talk openly within the movement and to the public about the repressive strategies I learn about in the course of my case, so that everyone can learn how the state is targeting activists.


To Take the Offense

: I will take an aggressive legal and media strategy to beat my case, call the state’s bluff, and politicize others.


To Pursue Collective Defense

: I will prioritize legal strategies leveraging collective defense so that we all beat the charges, together. I will encourage my lawyer to communicate with my co-defendants’ lawyers and other elements of the movement. When possible, I will utilize joint-defense agreements with my co-defendants.


Not to Denounce Others in the Movement

: I will not publicly denounce the tactical choices of anyone accused of actions I don’t personally agree with.


Not to Cooperate with Law Enforcement

: I will not cooperate with any investigatory or prosecutorial arm of the state. If I am pressured to do so, I will refuse. I will go public and tell the movement if law enforcement visits me.


Our goal is to make these ideas hegemonic. We want this pledge to reach far and wide. Print it out and read it with your friends. Paste it up at encampments. Go on the news and recite it. Distribute it at a No Kings march. Read it aloud at a court support event. Tag it across your city. Hang it by your front door. Get creative.

author: Unknown
title: The Student Revolt in France Spreads : Moving Forward with Rage and Solidarity
content:
October 17 marked one of the fiercest days of mass protest in recent French history. Scenes of ferocious resistance unfolded throughout the day, not only in Paris but in


Bordeaux

,


Dijon

,

Marseille

,

Nancy

, and dozens of other cities across the country. Some observers have described the day’s events as

more explosive

 than the

Yellow Vest movement

 of 2018-19—and the rebellion shows no sign of slowing.


How did we get here? Courageous high school students

have been protesting for weeks

 against abominable conditions in schools, the rise of the extreme right, and the bleak prospects they face in a world dominated by technocrats and tech barons. Alongside growing anti-government protests from

Albania

,

Italy

,

Spain

, and beyond in recent days, the French student rebellions may herald the emergence of a new wave of global struggle.


In this article, our correspondent from Paris explains the context behind the youth rebellion, tracks the movement’s growth over the two weeks leading up to October 17 and the government’s failed attempts to repress or to pacify it, and clarifies the stakes moving forward.


Stay tuned for a full report on the uprising of October 17 and the ongoing rebellions across France and beyond.


Thousands gather to protest police violence and support the students in revolt (Nantes, October 6, 2026)


This update on the student unrest in France picks up where we ended

our previous report

, on the eve of the national call to take the streets on October 6, 2026.


The stakes were high on this crucial day of action. It was critical to show massive solidarity with the high school students fighting like hell against the empty future looming on their horizon. The day presented an ideal opportunity to expand the scope of the current movement by joining forces to resist the authoritarian state power that has been growing stronger every day.


The following article provides further context and analysis to understand the current situation in France, along with reports on what went down in the streets over these last rebellious weeks.


Background: The

Banlieues

 and the Enemy Within


When governments or powerful institutions feel threatened, they often strive to reaffirm their authority by inventing scapegoats to hold responsible for all supposed misfortunes. By invoking the menace of an “enemy within,” politicians can shift blame for systemic problems that have resulted from their own actions onto a specific category of individuals. In France, the most common targets are the residents of the

banlieues

, the impoverished suburbs on the outskirts of Paris and other cities.


At the beginning of the student blockades, the movement remained limited to a handful of high schools in these Parisian suburbs. In response, President Emmanuel Macron and his ministers decided to react quickly and do everything in their power to silence this emerging wave of youth protest. Due to the location of the first blockades, authorities believed that they could act more freely and repress the unrest with impunity, since these specific territories have been targeted for generations by all government administrations across political lines.


The condition of the

banlieues

, which remain populated by descendants of the French Empire’s colonized subjects, reflects France’s ongoing role as a

neocolonial power

 that continues to exploit African territories. Consider the disastrous

oil project

 in Uganda orchestrated by the France-based multinational company TotalEnergies, or the

corruption case

 involving the French far-right business tycoon Vincent Bolloré and his bribery and money laundering schemes across West African ports.


French governments and corporations have no scruples about extracting enormous wealth from African countries. This neocolonial pillaging fuels France’s position as the

seventh richest country

 in the world today, according to the IMF. Yet despite these astronomical profits, the nation refuses to address the problems facing its post-colonial population and their descendants within its national territory.


At the twilight of France’s colonial empire, decades of occupation and racist violence had created political and economic instability across northern and western Africa. As a result, waves of migrants began leaving their countries to come to France for work in the 1950s. Upon arriving, they continued to face systemic colonial racism, relegated to the economic margins …

author: Valerie Anne
title: ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ Kicked Off Season 23 With a Sapphic Smooch
content:
Grey’s Anatomy came back with a bang. (Well, a smooch. But we’ll get there.) Amelia spent the entire episode getting the cold shoulder from Toni because, as I’m sure you remember, we left them last season with Toni showing up at Amelia’s door to profess her love for her, only to realize a naked Cass was already in Amelia’s apartment.

When we return for season 23(!), Toni is giving Amelia the cold shoulder all day. Amelia desperately wants to talk to her, but Toni isn’t hearing her out. They clash over work decisions, and Amelia starts to get frustrated. And at this point I was afraid the show was ending their storyline. I thought it was going to be a dramatic fight and then back to no wlw relationships on the show. I was thankfully wrong!

Eventually, the day leads Amelia to Toni’s front door, where she apologizes again for sleeping with Cass, and explains it was an emotional reaction to being so sure Toni was about get back together with her ex. She regrets it if it means she would lose Toni. She says she’s truly, madly, deeply in love with Toni and that if Toni is done, she’ll move on, but if not, she really doesn’t want to let what they have died. Toni considers her for a moment but then breaks; she’s still in love with Amelia, and she’s not done. The two kiss about it, and while I doubt their road ahead will be paved with roses and rainbows (especially because Toni’s ex is still in the picture, and goodness knows if/when Cass will return to drop bombs) but I’m glad we at least aren’t done with their story yet. I look forward to seeing what Season 23 will bring for our resident gays; here’s hoping none of them disappear into the parking lot of no return.

+ Olivia Rodrigo dropped a remix of her song “Expectations” with a verse by Chappell Roan in it, plus a music video go to alongside it (my TikTok FYP has been enjoying Chappell in the background singing, “not kissin’ no boy, NO BOY”)

+ Speaking of, Chappell Roan got to DJ and play Pink Pony Club at The Abbey, which inspired the song in the first place

+ Inde Navarrette, Janelle Monáe, Cole Escola, Amandla Stenberg, and more showed up in style at the Academy Museum gala

+ Future seasons of Ted Lasso are up in the air now that it has pivoted to a women’s team

author: Admin101
title: Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense
content:
Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN) is excited to announce the publication of

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

.


Drawing on organizing experiences of Black Rose/Rosa Negra members across the United States, this pamphlet explores how workers, neighbors, and communities are building collective resistance to ICE and defending their immigrant coworkers, classmates, and loved ones. By connecting struggles across workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, the

transversal organizing

 approach we prioritize builds solidarity across different sectors of society to confront the interconnected structures of domination that shape our lives.


You can find a downloadable PDF version of the pamphlet at the end of this text.


Two Years of Trump II: Immigrants in the Crosshairs, Resistance Under Attack


Upon returning to office, Donald Trump wasted little time fulfilling his white supremacist campaign pledge of “Mass Deportations Now.” Via a flurry of executive orders and congressional acts his administration reinstated the reviled “family separation” policy; directed virtually unlimited resources to stop a fictitious “invasion” of the country’s borders; and sought to end birthright citizenship. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents blitzed Los Angeles in June 2025 with spectacular raids, followed shortly by similar operations in dozens of cities across the country including New York City; Chicago, IL; New Orleans, LA; and Durham, NC. This “shock and awe” strategy culminated in Operation Metro Surge, a months-long invasion of the Minnesota Twin Cities that deported over 2,000 residents. 


Meanwhile, support for the deportation machine plummeted as collective action against it swelled. Everyday people covered their cars, lawns, and lips with the slogan “Abolish ICE;” as of July 2026, nearly 50% of US adults support such a measure. Both May Days since Trump’s second inauguration centered immigrant defense in their celebrations. Rapid-response networks that keep watch for ICE, document kidnappings, and sometimes disrupt them spread wildly. Know-your-rights training flourished at worksites and community centers. Millions of Red Cards–wallet-sized cards outlining the holder’s constitutional protections around interactions with ICE and other police–were distributed at schools, churches, restaurants, and municipal buildings. Children and their parents caged in concentration camps went on hunger strike as constituents bombarded politicians’ hotlines and town halls demanding humanitarian treatment and release outside their walls.


Popular responses in St. Paul and Minneapolis demonstrate the possibilities of mass resistance. Like the Los Angeles Tenant Union’s community defense centers that countered ICE’s Southern California invasion, organizers reactivated dormant neighborhood networks from the 2020 uprising and began building new ones when word spread that Commander-at-Large Greg Bovino was bringing his paramilitary forces to town. Once Operation Metro Surge launched, everyday Minnesotans refined sophisticated systems to track, delay, and disrupt arrests. ICE agents retaliated by killing rapid-responder Renée Good and shooting Julio C. Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant targeted for deportation. Instead of cowering from the naked clampdown, neighborhood networks coordinated with unions, churches, and other civil societal organizations to shut down their cities on January 23rd. In its wake, Trump ousted Bovino and immigration enforcement plummeted.


But July 2026 saw record high immigrant detentions since Trump’s return to office with little public opposition. What explains it? ICE’s tactical shifts undoubtedly played a role. Bovino replacement and “Border Czar” Tom Homan traded provocative street operations with quiet detainers at jails and prisons and “targeted operations” at sites protected from activist impediment like airports. Escalating repression has also raised the costs of resistance. ICE’s bevy of brutality has included intimidation, beatings, and shootings, culminating in murdering Good and rapid-responder Alex Pretti. Federal grand juries fish from the shadows for information about our movements, stoking fears of informants that slow our organizing. From the Prairieland defendants to the Minnesota 15 and more, indictments and convictions on flimsy charges could make prosecuting dissidents even easier. Evidentiary discovery in the …

author: Rafael Oliveira
title: Com “exército” de Janones, Lula consegue virada inédita e é reeleito presidente
content:
Nunca antes na história deste país, um candidato à presidência havia chegado ao segundo turno em desvantagem e revertido a posição.

 Aconteceu. Com 51,78% dos votos, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) está

reeleito

 presidente do Brasil e vai exercer seu quarto mandato.


A virada improvável, que envolveu uma redução inédita na abstenção entre um turno e o outro (de 21,08% para 19,22%), tem relação direta com uma mobilização sem precedentes nas redes sociais – justamente o terreno em que a

extrema direita

 deitou e rolou nos últimos anos.


A tomada das redes pelo campo progressista – que transbordou para as ruas, com as maiores manifestações da esquerda em décadas em todo o país – envolveu vários jovens parlamentares que subiram ao palanque do petista, como Ana Elisa, deputada federal eleita pelo PT em Minas Gerais aos 21 anos e Érika Hilton, reeleita pelo PSOL em São Paulo. Mas nenhuma figura se destacou tanto quanto a do deputado federal reeleito André Janones (Rede-MG) e seu canal do WhatsApp “Exército do Lula”, que soma quase 11 milhões de participantes.


Para os especialistas em comunicação e política ouvidos pela

Agência Pública

, é consenso que a estratégia digital capitaneada por Janones foi central na histórica virada de Lula.


Jornalismo investigativo é antídoto contra a desinformação. Ajude a garantir informação acessível e gratuita para mais pessoas. Faça um Pix para

contato@apublica.org

 ou doe em

apoie.apublica.org

.


“O Janones entendeu a lógica das plataformas [digitais], no sentido de que não adianta só fazer conteúdo impulsionado e ou divulgado por influenciadores.

 O trabalho de formiguinha das pessoas para os seus grupos, das pessoas para as suas redes, é muito importante”, aponta Raquel Recuero, coordenadora do Laboratório de pesquisa MIDIARS (Mídia, Discurso e Análise de Redes Sociais) da Universidade Federal de Pelotas (UfPel).


A pesquisadora destaca que a estratégia conduzida por Janones também acertou ao gerar rejeição a Flávio – algo que a extrema direita vinha fazendo desde o início do terceiro mandato de Lula. “O que mobilizou foi a emoção, o medo de uma vitória de Flávio Bolsonaro [PL]. Não existe comparação com a campanha do primeiro turno. Foi uma campanha muito mais abrangente, digital, que chegou muito mais nas pessoas, já que, querendo ou não, o espaço do debate hoje é o digital”, diz.


Recuero destaca ainda a relevância da campanha digital em um cenário adverso para Lula no Congresso. “A mobilização é importante porque mostra que o presidente eleito tem força de mobilização, ou seja, tem apoio popular, isso pressiona o Congresso, pressiona as instituições. Mas vai ser um governo difícil”, afirma.


A pesquisadora Maria Paula Almada, codiretora executiva do Aláfia Lab e doutora em Comunicação e Cultura Contemporâneas pela Universidade Federal da Bahia (Ufba), destaca as circunstâncias em que a virada histórica ocorreu, com denúncias de interferência por parte da

Meta

 e, de acordo com a pesquisadora, com “o ministro

Kassio Nunes Marques

 agindo de maneira dúbia, muitas vezes juridicamente equivocada, favorecendo claramente um dos lados”.


“A gente viveu, pela primeira vez na história do Brasil, uma eleição das bolhas, em que a gente não tinha acesso ao que o outro lado estava consumindo e tomando como percepção da realidade”, diz Almada.

“A gente sempre soube da importância das redes e sempre soube que a direita domina essa lógica, mas o papel dos algoritmos, das plataformas e o não acesso ao conteúdo que está sendo disseminado do outro lado é um fenômeno novo”

.


Para a pesquisadora, o fato de Lula ter ficado em segundo lugar em um primeiro turno morno, com uma esquerda desengajada, fez com que as pessoas começassem a se mobilizar, encarando um papel de “protagonistas”, com as missões desenvolvidas por Janones no canal de WhatsApp, o que foi central para reduzir a abstenção.


Tatiana Dourado, pesquisadora e professora do Programa de Pós-Graduação em Comunicação da PUC-Rio (PPGCOM PUC-Rio), destaca a importância da identificação na campanha vitoriosa de Lula. “O que vimos foi uma mobilização em larga escala, com milhões de pessoas acompanhando canais de WhatsApp e produzindo e compartilhando conteúdos virais que geravam identificação, ampliavam o alcance dessa onda e contribuíam para consolidar convicções de voto, que vão se reproduzindo por contágio”, descreve.


Ela aponta que essa identificação, para além do conteúdo racional, tem uma expressão emocional …

author: Administrador
title: Preparativos Zapatistas para el Encuentro Abrazo con familias Buscadoras. Parte 3: CUIDAR, PROTEGER, GUARDAR
content:
Música: Meme del Real, «El mundo en que nací» Imágenes, edición y producción: Terci@s Compas Zapatistas

Compañeras Familias Buscadoras:

Les saluda el Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés, coordinador general de la Gira por la Vida – Capítulo México.

Pues les comento que seguimos preparándonos para el viaje que haremos para conocerlas, y escuchar y aprender de sus dolores y resistencia. Y para guardar su palabra en nuestros corazones y en nuestra memoria. Esperamos, de veras, aprender mucho de ustedes.

Acá donde estamos concentrados, de repente llueve mucho y hace frío. Está bien para quienes vienen en tierras frías, pero los de tierra caliente, pues sufren un poco porque no están hallados. A la lluvia todos estamos bien hallados, porque de por sí acá en las montañas del sureste mexicano llueve mucho. Montaña adentro, en las lomas y la selva, llueve hasta cuando no llueve.

Unas con frío, otras con calor, las comunidades zapatistas han mandado a prepararse a delegadas, delegados y 3 delegadoas. Hasta ahora 1530 según la cuenta. Tal vez baja la cantidad por enfermedades o asuntos familiares. Por ejemplo, una compañera se sintió mal, la atendieron y salió en el ultrasonido que trae cría en su panza. Tuvo que regresar, por razón de que estén bien ella y su pichito. Pero rápido, un compañero que le sabe a eso de los tacos (de hacerlos, no de comerlos; porque de comerlos todos, todas y todoas estamos muy bien entrenados), rápido dijo que él entra de relevo. Y sí lo aprobaron las comandantas y comandantes porque de por sí escucha las pláticas que se dan para prepararnos bien.

Aquí en el video les mostramos unas de nuestras preparaciones.

Sea toda la delegación completa, sea en las partes en que nos organizamos, nos preparamos para marchas si es que hay o para mítines que les dicen. En esas marchas, si es que se hacen, nuestra principal preocupación no es el rollo que digamos, sino cuidar, guardar y proteger a las familias buscadoras. O sea que no vamos a la bulla, a echar relajo, sino a escuchar su palabra. Y pues tenemos que ver de cuidarlas porque en su corazón tienen palabras fuertes, duras, que enseñan y orientan en la lucha por la vida.

Y sabemos que aprenderemos porque llevamos nuestra libreta y nuestro lapicero. Y hasta computadoras y tabletas y celulares. Y van compañeras que les decimos “Tercias Compas” que le saben a eso de la cámara, la grabación, la edición y la transmisión de los encuentros. Pero lo más importante es que llevamos la cabeza, el corazón y las tripas con ganas de aprender.

Ahí pueden ver, en el video, que se ponen unas compañeras con sus pichitos como si fueran familias buscadoras marchando por verdad y justicia, y luego nuestra delegación o parte de nuestra delegación, camina a su lado y luego las envuelve en un como escudo.

Y hasta el Comando Palomitas practica de hacer el escudo que cuida, protege y guarda.

De por sí así nos enseñaron nuestros anteriores, que nos dijeron que somos guardianes y guardianas de la tierra, la madre más primera.

Como ven en las imágenes, con tanto lodo que se hace en las prácticas pues ya casi no es que marchamos, sino que como que nos deslizamos. Como patinando pues. Y luego pasa pues que la chancla se quedó atorada, o el tenis, y no se puede parar porque atrás viene la bola, el bulto de compas. Y entonces pues ni modos, hay que esperar a que termina la práctica para ir a buscar en el lodo, dónde es que quedó la chancla o el tenis. Y pues mientras andamos como chuchito renco.

Compañeras familias buscadoras:

No vamos a pasear. Vamos a abrazarlas si quieren, y si no, pues también vamos para oír su palabra.

Lo sabemos que hay gente que está mal hablando de la gira. Dividen, quieren decir quién sí y quién no puede reunirse con nosotros, o sea que quieren dejar fuera a otros grupos porque no se llevan, y cosas así. Ahí después, otro día, el Capitán Marcos les va a decir de eso hasta con nombres.

Por ahora sólo queremos mandarles nuestros respetos y cariño.

Desde las montañas del Sureste Mexicano. Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés. México, octubre del 2026.
