author: Randi Beers
title: Inuit Child First Initiative needs to be universal
content:
It was as simple as it was revolutionary.


In 2023,

somebody

 with the non-profit Indigenous Kids Network had the idea to help Clyde River apply for community-wide food vouchers, good for $500 per month per child under the age of 18, with an extra $250 per month allocated to children under four for needs such as diapers or formula.


Twenty-four of Nunavut’s 25 communities organized applications through the Inuit Child First Initiative. Once approved, Inuit families could declare how many children they had and receive cards loaded with money that they could use at their local grocers.


The Inuit Child First Initiative Hamlet Food Voucher program wasn’t really a program. It was an innovative way of using a pot of money meant to ensure Inuit children have equal access to health, social and education support.


Over the two years it was in place, the federal government

spent $89.5 million

 on vouchers that helped feed 15,000 Inuit children.


The effects were unequivocal. Parents who

reported

 they were eating one meal a day before the food vouchers were no longer skipping meals so their children could eat. Nunavut health-care workers

noticed

 a “night-and-day” change, with fewer children seeing doctors for nutrition-related issues. Teachers said students were more alert at school and their

grades improved

.


The food voucher program was staunched in early 2025 and Indigenous Services Canada rolled out stricter regulations for group requests.


These policy changes are also affecting the number of student support assistants in Nunavut schools this year, because Inuit Child First Initiative no longer approves requests for student support assistance, except for exceptional needs, again on a case-by-case basis.


Classrooms

look very different

 this year as a result, says Nunavut Teachers’ Association president Justin Matchett, with students not getting support and teachers struggling with stress and burnout.


Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty has been

working

 on a new-and-improved Inuit Child First Initiative for the past year. Hopefully she’s considering a more universal approach to the program.


The spirit and principle of Inuit Child First Initiative is to provide a safety net for Inuit children. Making it easy for organizations, schools and hamlets to get approval for group applications makes that safety net stronger and reduces the risk that individual families won’t walk away,

frustrated

 because of what at least one parent has described as an “inflexible, intrusive” application process that is “incompatible with life in Nunavut.”


Does a universal approach to Inuit Child First Initiative open the door for people to benefit from a program that might not be intended for them, such as more well-off families accessing food vouchers they may not need? Did the food voucher program contribute to food inflation in Nunavut? These were common criticisms.


Abuse of open-ended programs is, of course, possible.


But Inuit Child First Initiative needs to meet Nunavummiut where they are. And laborious, extensive applications that require documentation and endorsements are not feasible for many families.


We know the food voucher program and other group-focused initiatives led to healthier Inuit children.


Reinstating the old Inuit Child First Initiative won’t fix everything.


But it would be a grievous mistake to, in the name of saving a little money now, forgo

positive impacts

 that lead to better health outcomes — and money saved down the line.

author: Unknown
title: YJA Star: We are the inheritors of Bêrîtan’s legacy
content:
The Central Headquarters Command of the Free Women’s Troops (YJA Star) commemorated guerrilla commander Gülnaz Karataş, known by her nom de guerre Bêrîtan Hêvî, highlighting her significance for the Kurdish women’s freedom movement on the 34th anniversary of her death. In a statement on Saturday, YJA Star Command paid tribute to Bêrîtan Hêvî’s resistance against surrender during the Southern War of 1992, describing her political and military legacy as one of the foundations of Kurdish women’s autonomous organization.


Bêrîtan Hêvî was born in 1971 in Bingöl, North Kurdistan, and died on October 25, 1992, in the Xakurke region of South Kurdistan. During clashes between PKK guerrillas and Peshmerga forces allied with the Turkish army, she was surrounded by members of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP). She refused to surrender, fought until her last bullet, destroyed her weapon, and jumped from a cliff to avoid capture.


Her death became an important reference point in the development of autonomous women’s structures within the guerrilla movement. On November 1, 1993, the establishment of a women’s army was announced. YJA Star sees itself as continuing this development and the tradition of resistance among Kurdish women, which it traces from Dersim to the present day.


The full statement by the YJA Star Central Headquarters Command reads as follows:


“Bêrîtan embodies the reality of women who organize and liberate themselves, establish their own identity, and express it through their lives. She represents women’s struggle for their existence within the Kurdish freedom movement, the lived and realized reality of women who lead a people’s struggle for freedom, and their stance against subjugation.


The fact that the spirit of resistance of the women who defied subjugation during the Dersim massacre and threw themselves from cliffs took shape once again in Bêrîtan represents the continuity of a tradition of resistance. The spirit of Besê and the women of Dersim found its expression in Bêrîtan and came to life anew in the struggle of the present day.


Bêrîtan represents the fighting woman who resisted surrender in the 1992 war against reactionary Kurdish collaborationism and whose resistance unfolded at the edge of a precipice. Through her determined stance against collaboration and betrayal, she also laid a foundation, as a woman, for the unity and collective action of the Kurdish people.


“Fight, my rose, fight with determination”


Through her ideological awareness, Bêrîtan developed a strong stance. She acquired strategic and tactical skills, advanced as a commander, and put her convictions into practice. In doing so, she embodied the standards, principles, and political line of the fighting woman.


With the words,

“Fight, my rose, fight with determination. By fighting, we liberate ourselves; by liberating ourselves, we become beautiful; and the more beautiful we become, the more we are loved,”

she expressed the holistic development of the individual and the path of struggle. Through her stance and actions, she became a guiding figure in the women’s freedom movement. She demonstrated once again that the establishment of a women’s army and the struggle cannot be reduced to armed resistance alone, but require a conscious stance and a profound understanding of one’s own reality.


Through her life, she transformed the aesthetics of struggle, the ethics of resistance, and the standards and principles of love into a manifesto. Bêrîtan inscribed her life and struggle into history, verse by verse. She gave voice once again, at the very edge of the precipices, to the existence of women who were meant to be buried in history and condemned to silence in the depths of the abyss. From there, she carried the cry of women’s resistance to all women. With the words,

“The revolution demands a stormy personality,”

 she continually recreated herself through resistance against backward traditions and collaborationism. With every bullet she fired and every chain of enslavement she shattered, she unleashed new storms. Like a poem, she inscribed the truth of women’s resistance into history and gave it a distinct identity.


A legacy for the women’s freedom movement


Through her struggle, Bêrîtan not only wrote the manifesto of her own time. She also gave new meaning to the legacy of the women whose heritage she had inherited—the Besês. She left future generations the consciousness of a commander and a vision of resistance …

author: Unknown
title: Democratic Integration Conference in Zurich discusses democratic transformation, equal coexistence
content:
The Kurdish Social Research Association (Akademî Kurd) is holding a conference titled “Democratic Integration” in Zurich, Switzerland. The conference, taking place at the Kirchgemeindehaus, is examining the concept of democratic integration from various perspectives within the framework of LAbdullah Öcalan’s Manifesto for a Democratic Communal Society.


The conference, attended by academics, politicians, legal experts, and researchers, focuses on the theoretical foundations of democratic integration as well as its social, political, and cultural dimensions. Legal reforms necessary for a democratic resolution of the Kurdish question, equal citizenship, the democratic republic, and the democratic communal economy are also among the main topics of discussion.


Dilan Çetinkaya: The process places significant responsibilities on all of us


The conference began with a minute of silence in memory of the martyrs of the revolutionary struggle, followed by an opening speech delivered by Dilan Çetinkaya, Co-Chair of the Democratic Kurdish Council of Switzerland (CDK-S).


Dilan Çetinkaya began her speech by commemorating the martyrs of the Kurdish Freedom Struggle and drew attention to the Kurdish people’s struggle for freedom spanning more than half a century. Stating that this struggle has brought significant gains to the Kurdish people, Çetinkaya emphasized the historical importance of the peace and democratic society process initiated under the leadership of Abdullah Öcalan.


Çetinkaya stated that the ongoing process places significant responsibilities not only on political actors but also on all segments of society, stressing that democratic transformation must be reflected in every aspect of life. “Change must not remain merely in words; it must take place in every sphere. We must thoroughly understand Leader Öcalan’s concept of democratic integration and carry out our reconstruction accordingly,” she said.


Veysi Aktaş: Democratic integration is based on the democratic transformation of all peoples


Following the opening speech, the conference proceeded to its first session, titled “The conceptual and theoretical framework of democratic integration.” Moderated by Gülistan Arslan, the session featured Kurdish politician Veysi Aktaş and sociologist, academic, and author Nazan Üstündağ as speakers.


Veysi Aktaş began by thanking Akademî Kurd for organizing the conference. Stating that democratic integration is one of the fundamental concepts of the peace and democratic society process, Aktaş said that the concept points not only to the resolution of existing problems but also to the building of a democratic future in which peoples can live together in equality and freedom.


Aktaş explained that democratic integration is based on different identities and social groups creating a shared democratic life while preserving their distinct identities. “Democratic integration is a concept based on the democratic transformation of all peoples, not just the Kurds. It is founded on coexistence with differences, equality, equal negotiation as a method, and democratic participation,” he said.


Emphasizing that democratic integration does not mean assimilation or the elimination of differences, Aktaş stated that the concept is fundamentally based on the recognition of different identities, social pluralism, and democratic participation. In this respect, he explained that democratic integration entails not only the recognition of the political and social rights of Kurds but also the restructuring of society as a whole on a democratic basis.


‘The fundamental principle is equal citizenship’


Remarking that democratic integration rests on several fundamental principles, Aktaş said that equal citizenship is foremost among them. He emphasized that equal citizenship cannot be understood merely as formal equality before the law, highlighting the importance of enabling different identities and social groups to participate in political and social life while preserving their distinct characteristics.


Aktaş stated that democratic integration is directly linked to the perspective of a democratic republic and stressed the need to establish legal guarantees to ensure that democratic transformation becomes lasting.


“Democratic integration is also based on the Democratic Republic. Achieving this is possible through the implementation of a legal process. Certain legal reforms are necessary for it to become a reality in everyday life,” he …

author: Unknown
title: KOMAW calls for international action against death sentence for Varisheh Moradi
content:
The Association of Families of Martyrs and the Disappeared (KOMAW) called on international institutions to intervene against the renewed death sentence imposed on Kurdish activist Varisheh Moradi. In a statement, the organization condemned the Iranian regime’s execution policy and the ongoing repression of women, political activists, and opposition groups. KOMAW has submitted a dossier on Moradi’s case and other human rights violations in Iran to international institutions.


In November 2024, Branch 15 of the Revolutionary Court in Tehran sentenced Moradi to death on charges of “rebellion against the state.” The Supreme Court overturned the ruling in December 2025 due to serious deficiencies in the investigation. Instead of conducting the additional investigations ordered by the Supreme Court, the same court branch once again imposed the death penalty in mid-October. The defense has described the proceedings as unlawful and rejected the accusations against Moradi. The new verdict is not yet final.


KOMAW views the proceedings as another manifestation of the systematic oppression of the Kurdish population in particular, as well as other communities in Iran. “Women who fight for freedom, equality, and democratic rights are particularly vulnerable to persecution and severe punishment. However, human rights must not be sacrificed to political power interests or ideological conflicts.”


Dossier submitted to international institutions


Through the dossier, KOMAW aims to prompt the United Nations (UN) human rights mechanisms, as well as international women’s and human rights organizations, to take action against Moradi’s threatened execution and the ongoing violations of rights in Iran. The documents are intended to initiate independent investigations and diplomatic initiatives. The association announced that it would monitor responses to its submissions and keep the international public informed of further developments.


Six demands to the international community


In its statement, KOMAW outlined six specific demands. The first is the immediate annulment of the death sentence against Moradi and the prevention of its enforcement. The association also calls for independent investigations into executions, allegations of torture, arbitrary arrests, and politically motivated judicial proceedings in Iran. The relevant UN bodies and international human rights organizations are urged to continuously monitor developments.


At the same time, KOMAW calls for stronger diplomatic measures against Tehran to halt executions and ensure the protection of fundamental freedoms. It also calls for political, diplomatic, and economic relations with Iran to be reviewed from a human rights perspective. As its sixth demand, the association calls for effective protection of women’s rights activists and human rights defenders against persecution, ill-treatment, and the threat of execution.

author: Bruno Malheiro
title: The Destruction of the Amazon Is Central to the Bolsonaros’ Vision for Brazil
content:
Flávio Bolsonaro may revive his father’s program to transform the Amazon into ranches, strip mines, and plantations.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Bolsonarismo wasn’t born at the ballot box. Before it became an electoral force, it had already been taking shape along the frontiers of Brazilian capitalism, through the expansion of a territorial logic that subordinated land, nature and social relations to private accumulation. That logic legitimized the destruction of common resources and delegitimized other ways of organizing life. In 2018, maps of soy production, cattle ranching and mining overlapped with the maps showing where Jair Bolsonaro won his strongest electoral results. That wasn’t a cartographic coincidence. These frontiers were tied to political and cultural circuits, ranging from agribusiness fairs to shooting clubs to religious networks, that spread an unrestricted defense of private property, the promise of prosperity and the ideology of individual entrepreneurship. As commodity production homogenized landscapes, it also homogenized behavior and social narratives, weakening people’s ties to the land, to memory and to collective life. In the end, “agro” became “pop,” taking a central place in how meaning gets produced in Brazil.

The destruction of the Amazon is the most brutal expression of this territorial logic. Felled forests, poisoned rivers, invaded territories, and people driven out or killed: none of this is a side effect of development. These are the direct results of processes that subordinate life to private accumulation and delegitimize other ways of organizing territory. These processes sustain power relations that have expanded the far right’s strength, reach and legitimacy, and the 2018 election gave it a path into the Brazilian state.

Between 2019 and 2022, these geographies scaled up to the level of state policy, turning the Amazon into a laboratory for authoritarian experimentation. Relaxed environmental regulations, weakened enforcement, attacks on territorial rights, and the legitimization of violence in defense of private property all expanded the conditions for destruction. During this period, accumulated deforestation in the Legal Amazon reached 45,612 square kilometers, according to Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research (Inpe) and its Amazon deforestation monitoring program, known as Prodes, in 2022. The Bolsonaro administration’s agricultural policy encouraged bringing more land into the market and drove land re-concentration, while Funai, Ibama and ICMBio, Brazil’s Indigenous affairs, environmental protection and biodiversity conservation agencies, were all weakened, and environmental policy became increasingly militarized. Illegal mining expanded into Indigenous territories, linked to organized crime and enabled by the state’s tolerance. The Yanomami crisis captured this policy in its starkest form: more than 20,000 illegal miners invaded Yanomami territory, worsening river contamination and spreading disease, hunger and death, all while the government looked away.

In the Amazon, this offensive brought together sectors of traditional oligarchies with new political actors tied to predatory economic interests, including illegal ones connected to organized crime. These actors converted their economic interests into electoral power under the banner of bolsonarismo. Brazil’s so called secret budget strengthened local groups and leaders, expanding the far right’s reach across the region’s interior. This consolidation also relied on political violence, attacks on the press and the intimidation of opponents, all of which restricted critical thought and made it harder for left wing forces to organize. The Amazonian experience shows how the Bolsonaro project reshaped Brazilian patrimonialism, brought private interests closer to an authoritarian agenda and narrowed the conditions under which democracy could function.

Lula won the 2022 election by a narrow margin. His government rebuilt institutions, restored public policies, rebuilt state capacity and put Amazon protection back on the federal agenda. Brazil also regained ground in multilateral diplomacy, working to defend its interests across different blocs without aligning itself with a single center of power, a significant stance in an international landscape marked by wars and geopolitical disputes …

author: Randi Beers
title: News quiz Oct. 24 | Time for an education
content:
It’s time for another news quiz. You ready? Let’s go!


1.

 Gjoa Haven’s Emerald Hatkaittuq travelled to Manitoulin Island in September as part of her journalism studies. What was out of the ordinary about the trip?


A.

 Her group encountered a black bear while on the island but luckily they were equipped with bear spray.


B.

 Hatkaittuq’s flight back was delayed by weather, leaving her stranded in Yellowknife for a week.


C.

 She had the chance to interview Tom Selleck, who owns a home near Manitoulin Island.


2.

 A man in Qikiqtarjuaq forfeited his right to a jury trial in September. What happened?


A.

 He slept in and did not showed up late to the first day of his trial, causing a mistrial.


B.

 He heckled the jurors.


C.

 He simply stated he no longer wanted a jury trial, so the judge scheduled a new trial by judge alone.


3.

 People in Iqaluit might hear blasting this month as workers make room for what potential development?


A.

 A new movie theatre


B.

 A new Ampere building


C.

 A mall


4.

 Cst. Jerry Patterson is Nunavik Police Service’s newest Inuk recruit. Why did he decide to become a police officer?


A.

 He loves detective movies.


B.

 The pay is good, and the work allows for travel.


C.

 His father was an officer, and he wanted to follow in his footseps.


5.

 Nunavut classrooms look different this year, says Justin Matchett, president of the Nunavut Teachers’ Association. Why?


A.

 All classrooms are fitted with brand new smart boards.


B.

 There are fewer student support assistants, causing stress and burnout among teachers.


C.

 There are many more Inuit teachers thanks to a new recruiting initiative.


Alanna Dean, left, interviews fellow student Emerald Hatkaittuq while testing audio recording equipment during an in-person intensive for Carleton University’s Certificate in Journalism in Indigenous Communities on Manitoulin Island, Ont., in September. (Photo by Cedar Grace Photography)


Answers:


1.

 B — Hatkaittuq was

stranded

 in Yellowknife on her way back to Gjoa Haven. Her Carleton University program director Duncan McCue noted how far Hatkaittuq had to travel to get to Manitoulin Island, but was happy the university was able to support her trip.


2.

 A — Ronald Aulakiak did not set an alarm,

slept in

, and failed to make it to his own trial. He tried to argue he hadn’t forfeited his right to a jury trial, but the judge sided with the Crown, saying sleeping in is not a reasonable excuse to miss your own trial.


3.

 B — Ampere is hoping to

build

 an expanded Makerspace Economic Development Hub along the Road to Nowhere. The not-for-profit provides educational programming for people of all ages.


4.

 C — Allen Patterson

served as an officer

 with the Kativik Regional Police when his son Jerry Patterson was a child. “I spent my entire youth watching my dad be a cop,” Jerry Patterson said. “It inspired me to pursue that path.”


5.

 B — Thanks to a

change

 in how Inuit Child First Initiative funding requests are approved, there are fewer student support assistants working in Nunavut classrooms. It’s causing stress, says Justin Matchett, president of the Nunavut Teachers’ Association, because teachers have to manage their own curriculum and have less help with students who have special needs.

author: Shahad Ali
title: Netanyahu May Lose Israeli Elections. That Won’t Save Gaza From Occupation.
content:
As living conditions here in Gaza deteriorate, we have little hope that Israel’s elections will ease our suffering.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Israel is scheduled to hold general elections on October 27, with a fierce contest between incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the Likud party, and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party. These will be the first elections since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks on Israel.

The continuation of suffering in Gaza has been exploited as a political tool to attract more votes in Israel’s electoral struggle. The Likud party, led by Netanyahu, has cited ongoing military operations and the assassinations of Palestinian faction leaders in Gaza as evidence that its military strategy is working, warning that its opponents would end the war without fully destroying Hamas. It also frames the election as a decisive battle to protect Israel from the establishment of a Palestinian state and prevent the Palestinian Authority from returning to govern Gaza. The party argues that an opposition victory would mean yielding to international pressure and accepting a two-state solution.

Likud’s campaign rhetoric has unfolded alongside calls from its far right coalition partners for the “voluntary emigration” of Palestinians from Gaza and the re-establishment of Israeli settlements in the Strip. Both Bezalel Smotrich, Israel’s finance minister and leader of the Religious Zionism party, and Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s national security minister and leader of the Jewish Power party, have championed rebuilding Israeli settlements in Gaza since October 7, 2023, framing the war as an opportunity to reverse the 2005 disengagement. Moreover, as part of his election campaign, Ben-Gvir has proposed a seven-year plan, which he calls “Disengagement 710,” to relocate approximately 1.86 million Palestinians from Gaza.

On the other hand, Gadi Eisenkot, the main challenger to Netanyahu and leader of Israel’s Yashar party, pledged to remove Hamas from power in Gaza and destroy its military wing within 18 months of becoming prime minister. Speaking near the Gaza border, he said he would work to end Hamas’s rule in the Strip, either by implementing U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan, which Netanyahu’s government had approved, or through military force.

In Gaza, most people see no real difference between Benjamin Netanyahu and rivals such as Gadi Eisenkot. In our view, Gaza’s future will not be determined at the Israeli ballot box. Both Netanyahu’s and Eisenkot’s parties and members of their coalition are likely to pursue similar policies toward our cause. Although the leading parties may have different ideas and methods, their policies ultimately serve the same goal: destroying Gaza and reshaping its reality and culture to give it an Israeli character.

As the election approaches, humanitarian conditions in Gaza continue to deteriorate. Israeli forces are intensifying their military operations across the Strip through airstrikes, artillery fire, and the expansion of the area under their control, known as the Yellow Line. Since the ceasefire agreement was announced on October 10, 2025, ongoing Israeli attacks have killed 1,522 Palestinians and injured 5,421 others. Israeli forces now control an estimated 63 percent to 70 percent of the Strip and continue to seize additional land. Recently reported expansion into more areas of eastern Gaza City has forced many families to flee without a suitable place to go.

The International Organization for Migration warns that approximately 1.8 million people in Gaza face a fourth winter without adequate protection from rain, flooding, and cold. Meanwhile, Israeli authorities continue to block the entry of emergency shelter supplies, timber for repairs, heating equipment, and winter clothing through the crossings.

In addition to this, the Israeli Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) announced in a statement on October 15 that coordination for the entry of commercial goods into Gaza had been suspended. COGAT claimed that the decision was made by local merchants in Gaza, who had grown frustrated with Hamas’s imposition of taxes on their trucks. However, Jihad Esleem, deputy head of the Private Transport Association in Gaza, announced on October 19 that an official agreement had …

author: Mike Ludwig
title: Courts Reject Trump’s Attempt at Deploying ICE to Intimidate Voters
content:
A judge ordered Homeland Security to stop sending agents door to door in nine key states to hunt for “voter fraud.”

A judge ordered Homeland Security to stop sending agents door to door in nine key states to hunt for “voter fraud.”

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The Trump administration is attempting to intimidate Latino voters and naturalized citizens with the threat of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids and arrests ahead of the midterm elections, democracy advocates are warning.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, has deployed federal agents in multiple states to knock on doors and demand voters verify their identities and registration as part of an “Unlawful Voter Initiative” launched in August. In response to a lawsuit filed on October 19 by labor and voting rights groups, a federal judge in California ruled the DHS initiative violates the Voting Rights Act and ordered federal agents to halt “elections-related field operations and field interviews” in California, Wisconsin, New York, Missouri, Connecticut, Nevada, Georgia, Pennsylvania, and Washington.

“I look at this list of states, and I can think of some high-profile races that may be anticipated to be close in a lot of those jurisdictions,” said David Janovsky, senior policy analyst and acting director of the Constitution Project at the Project On Government Oversight, in an interview. “So, I think there is a reasonable question in all of this about how the federal government is choosing to focus these efforts, and the motivation that is behind that.”

Critical contests in these states include the tight race between Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and Republican Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia, which could decide which party has a majority in the Senate. In California, New York, and beyond, multiple races could help to determine control of the House or pad a Democratic majority.

Janovsky said sending agents door-to-door in states where Republicans face headwinds could suppress turnout. Indeed, since the 2024 election, polls suggest that Latinos and many other voters turned against the GOP as ICE invaded major cities such as Chicago and Minneapolis, causing chaos, fear, and death.

By deploying federal immigration agents to go door-to-door hunting for so-called “voter fraud” ahead of Election Day, the Trump administration may also be preparing the ground for meddling with election results and suppressing dissent if Republicans perform poorly and lose their congressional majority.

With billions of dollars in funding from Congress, the Trump administration has transformed ICE into a powerful tool of intimidation. ICE agents have injured and killed people in multiple high-profile cases since Donald Trump took office again. Under Trump’s mass deportation campaign, ICE has detained at least 506 U.S. citizens as well as many legal permanent residents. People arrested by ICE are often jailed in facilities where dozens have died amid complaints of medical neglect, including a lawful permanent resident who was found dead in a Texas ICE jail last week.

Trump’s Justice Department has been trying for over a year to get voter rolls from every state and hand them over to DHS investigators searching for evidence of widespread fraud that experts say does not exist. DHS uses voter data to create “target lists” of potentially fraudulent voter registrations, according to Wednesday’s court order.

“With Homeland Security agents knocking on people’s doors asking them if they are properly registered to vote, there is a very real concern, and it’s pretty well known, that the federal government doesn’t have accurate data,” Janovsky said. “It could freak people out, like, ‘maybe I don’t want to register to vote and put myself on this list.’”

Under an executive order issued in May 2025, the Department of Justice demanded voter rolls from states to share with DHS so agents could scour for non-citizens attempting to vote, which is exceedingly rare. States run elections, not the federal government, but many red states handed voter data over voluntarily. Another 26 states, including those named in Wednesday’s order, saw lawsuits filed by the Justice Department over voter rolls dismissed by federal courts.

“That effort has largely been rejected by the courts, because basically the federal government has no real business micromanaging every state’s voter rolls,” …

author: Solange Guimarães
title: Nunes Marques faz TSE pender para Flávio Bolsonaro ao priorizar decisões e conduzir pautas
content:
O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) sob o comando do atual presidente, ministro Kassio Nunes Marques, tem garantido à campanha eleitoral de Flávio Bolsonaro tratamento diferenciado. Mas para isso, precisou abrir mão de sua isonomia, segundo quatro especialistas ouvidos pela

Agência Pública

: o advogado e professor de Direito Eleitoral da Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV-SP), Fernando Neisser, a professora de Direito Eleitoral na Universidade de Brasília (UnB), Caroline Lacerda, o constitucionalista e professor da PUC-SP Pedro Serrano e Aldo Fornazieri, coordenador do curso de pós-graduação em Estratégia e Liderança Política da Fundação Escola de Sociologia e Política de São Paulo (FESPSP). 


O funcionamento da Corte apresenta “um desequilíbrio no tratamento [entre os candidatos]”, “assimetria [na comparação entre as campanhas]”, “uma postura claramente anti-isonômica” e “um viés em favor da candidatura de Flávio Bolsonaro evidente”, dizem os entrevistados, respectivamente.


O responsável pelo quadro, na visão tanto de Neisser como de Fornazieri, é o atual presidente do TSE. “Não tenho dúvida alguma que está havendo um desequilíbrio no tratamento, fundamentalmente por parte da Presidência [do TSE] e algumas vezes também por parte do ministro André Mendonça”, afirma Neisser.


“E mais grave, está havendo o uso estratégico da pauta por parte do presidente [Nunes Marques]. Decisões que beneficiariam o Lula, às vezes em plenário virtual, já com maioria formada, Ele apresenta destaque, retira de pauta”, complementa o professor da FGV.


Kassio Nunes Marques foi indicado ao Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) pelo então presidente Jair Bolsonaro, em novembro de 2020. Já ministro, em março de 2025, votou contra O ministro Nunes Marques, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), votou contra recursos do ex-presidente e do general Braga Netto para impedir os ministros Alexandre de Moraes, Flávio Dino e Cristiano Zanin de atuarem em seus julgamentos por tentativa de golpe de Estado. O julgamento ocorreu e ambos foram condenados.


Atualmente, Nunes Marques está envolvido em várias denúncias de envolvimento com o caso Master e o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro. Entre elas, a denúncia da

revista piauí

 de mudar votos em processos no STF que beneficiaram negócios do Banco. Uma outra

reportagem da revista piauí

 também indica que Vorcaro teria organizado uma festa em seu apartamento de luxo em São Paulo para receber o ministro.  


Outra forma de beneficiar a campanha de um candidato é segurar as decisões referentes a outra campanha.

“As representações propostas pela campanha do Lula têm demorado a ser julgadas, independentemente do tema, mais do que as propostas pelo Flávio”

 diz Neisser. 


Uma pesquisa do professor de Direito Celso de Oliveira Santos, da Universidade do Estado do Rio de Janeiro (Uerj), divulgada pelo

Estadão

, identificou que 25,7% das ações apresentadas por Flávio Bolsonaro receberam decisão em até três dias no segundo turno, contra 19,8% das movidas por Lula.


O gabinete de Nunes concentrou 43,3% das ações de Lula contra Flávio, mas apenas 16,8% das apresentadas pelo candidato do PL contra o petista. Entre as 38 ações de Lula que já haviam completado três dias de tramitação, nenhuma tinha recebido decisão nesse intervalo. Das 15 ações de Flávio nas mesmas condições, uma havia sido decidida.


A diferença ganha importância porque, numa eleição disputada nas redes sociais, uma decisão que chega tarde pode não ter qualquer efeito. Uma publicação retirada do ar durante os últimos dias da campanha pode perder seu alcance mesmo que a proibição seja revogada depois.


“A ação judicial virou ferramenta de comunicação”, explica Lacerda. Para a professora, durante uma campanha eleitoral, a demora ao analisar um caso “tem efeito prático de indeferimento.

 Se o pedido só é analisado depois que o conteúdo já circulou, ou depois da eleição, quem pediu perdeu, mesmo sem nenhuma decisão contrária”, explica. “Então a diferença de ritmo produz, sim, desequilíbrio entre as campanhas”, complementa.


Para ela, o resultado político de uma liminar pode ser mais importante do que a decisão definitiva: “Numa eleição apertada, deixar um vídeo forte fora do ar por alguns dias pode valer mais do que ganhar o processo depois”.


A dimensão dessa disputa aparece também nos números do

Núcleo Jornalismo

. Com base em dados abertos do TSE, o veículo identificou, até 20 de outubro, pelo menos 353 processos relacionados a reclamações digitais ou …

title: Έκθεση: Ο μυστικός Τύπος της αντίστασης στη ναζιστική κατοχή
content:
Έκθεση για τον μυστικό Τύπο της Εθνικής Αντίστασης


Φέτος, συμπληρώνονται 82 χρόνια από την απελευθέρωση της Θεσσαλονίκης, στις 30 Ὀκτωβρίου1944, από τα γερμανικά στρατεύματα Κατοχής, με την καταλυτική επέμβαση των ανταρτικών δυνάμεων του ΕΛΑΣ, που έσωσαν και τις υποδομές της πόλης από την καταστροφὴ.


Η Εταιρεία

Διάσωσης ι

στορικὡν

Αρχεἱων Μακεδονίας


(EΔΙA)

1940-1974,

τιμώντας την επέτειο ’απολὐτρωσης’ της πόλης από το ναζιστικό ζυγό, διοργανώνει, από τις 19-29|1Ο|2026͵στο χώρο του φουαγιέ του Δημαρχείου Θεσσαλονίκης,

έκθεση για τον μυστικὸ Τύπο της Εθνικἠς Αντίστασης

, που κυκλοφόρησε την περίοδο 1941-1944 στη Θεσσαλονίκη και την υπόλοιπη Βόρεια Ελλάδα.


Στα μαύρα χρόνια της χιτλερικής σκλαβιᾶς τηνπερίοδο 1941—1944, κυκλοφὀρησαν περισσότερες από 220 μυστικές εφηµερίδες στους νομούς της Μακεδονίας και της Θράκης. ‘Εναςπραγµατικός’άθλος’, αν σκεφτεί κανείς τις ανείπωτες δυσκολίες και τους θανάσιμους κινδύνους της Κατοχής, όταν και μόνο ηανάγνωση κάποιας αντιστασιακής εφημερίδας μπορούσε να καταλήξει στο εκτελεστικό απόσπασμα των Ναζί κατακτητών.


Το αρχειακό υλικό που εκτίθεται, προέρχεται από τη συλλογή του δημοσιογρἀφου-ιστορικού ερευνητή Σπύρου Κουζινόπουλου. Η έκθεση πραγματοποιείται υπό την αιγίδα του ΔήμουΘεσσαλονίκης και μετην ευγενική υποστήριξη του Οργανισμού Μεγάρου Μουσικής Θεσσαλονίκης.


Η έκθεση είναι ανοιχτή στο κοινό όλες τις μέρες της εβδομάδας, από τις 10π.μ. έως τις 8.30μ.μ.͵Σάββατο-Κυριακἠ έως τις 6.30μ.μ.


Σημειώνεται ότι η 30η Ὀκτωβρίου, ημέρα απελευθέρωσης της πόλης από τα χιτλερικά στρατεύματα κατοχής, καθιερώθηκε ως “δηµόσια εορτἠ τοπικής σημασίας για τον Δἠμο Θεσσαλονίκης’ με το Προεδρικό Διάταγμα 50|9-5-2016.

title: PKK prisoners: We accept neither forced expressions of remorse nor delays in our release
content:
PKK prisoners in Turkish prisons have strongly criticized the continued obstruction of prisoner releases, the practice of forcing prisoners to express remorse, and the lack of political steps in the peace and democratic society process. In a statement signed by Deniz Kaya, they called on the Turkish government to fulfill its responsibility for a democratic resolution of the Kurdish question, remove legal and political obstacles, and create the conditions for the freedom of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan.


The statement focuses on the decisions of prison Administrative and Observation Boards, which prevent prisoners from being released even after they have served their regular prison sentences. The prisoners particularly reject demands that they renounce their political beliefs or express remorse in order to regain their freedom. They also recall the history of resistance among Kurdish prisoners, particularly in Diyarbakır (Kurdish: Amed) Prison following the military coup of September 12, 1980.


The full statement on Saturday reads as follows:


Delays in the peace process weaken the will to find a solution


“The current peace and democratic society process has opened the door to a historic phase in which our peoples’ hopes for a free, equal, and democratic life are growing. The determination Abdullah Öcalan has demonstrated to advance this process, end armed confrontations, and develop a democratic political solution, as well as the steps he has taken toward these goals, are evident.


Restricting the fundamental issues of a democratic solution to the framework of security measures, postponing legal reforms, and prolonging the process by making it conditional on certain requirements do not strengthen the will to find a solution but instead undermine it. Such an approach risks deepening existing deadlocks rather than paving the way for a solution.


It is clear that peace cannot be achieved through statements alone but requires concrete steps, mutual responsibility, and an approach that places democratic transformation at its core. If this new phase is truly intended to mark the beginning of democratic change, the benchmark must not be a redefinition of security policy. Rather, what matters is that the state demonstrates its willingness to democratize itself through concrete, practical steps.


Arbitrary obstruction of prisoner releases


The current stance of the state and government, which involves prolonging the process and delaying concrete steps under various pretexts, is incompatible with the peace and democratic society process. This is particularly evident in the violations of rights in prisons, the continued delays in prisoner releases, the unresolved situation of sick prisoners, and the forced declarations of remorse imposed through decisions by the Administrative and Observation Boards.


It is unacceptable that the situation of our comrades who have been imprisoned for decades and have already served their legally prescribed sentences is subjected to arbitrary assessments and political conditions. When subjective judgments replace legal guarantees, prisoners’ rights are restricted through administrative mechanisms, and their releases are postponed indefinitely, serious concerns arise regarding the principles of law and justice.


The situation of all our comrades whose release is being obstructed, particularly sick prisoners, must be addressed on the basis of human rights and the guarantees of the rule of law.


We reject the policy of forced expressions of remorse


As imprisoned members of the PKK movement, we explicitly declare that we will not accept any approach aimed at breaking our will. We reject both the policy of forced declarations of remorse imposed by the Administrative and Observation Boards and measures intended to pressure us into abandoning our convictions. For us, freedom is not a right that can be made dependent on the approval of a committee, a declaration of remorse, or the expectations of those in political power. Freedom is inseparably linked to human dignity, democratic life, and fundamental human rights.


The tradition of resistance from Amed to the present day


Our history of struggle is a history of resistance against subjugation and of the determination to achieve freedom in the face of policies of denial and annihilation. The experience of fifty years of struggle represents a tradition of resistance forged through great sacrifices and our people’s pursuit of freedom …

title: JetBlue'da finansal baskı arttı
content:
Fotoğraf: Mertbiol/Wikimedia Commons CC0

İran savaşının ardından artan yakıt maliyetleri, ABD’li havayolu şirketi JetBlue üzerindeki finansal baskıyı daha da artırdı.

The Wall Street Journal’ın haberine göre, JetBlue’nun büyük alacaklılarından oluşan bir grup, şirket üzerindeki finansal baskıların artması üzerine finansal yeniden yapılandırma seçeneklerini değerlendirmek için finansal danışmanlık kuruluşu PJT Partners ile çalışmaya başladı.

Reuters’ın haberine göre, bilet fiyatlarının artmasına ve havayolu seyahat talebinin sabit kalmasına rağmen, İran savaşının ardından uçak yakıtı maliyetlerindeki keskin artış, ABD’li havayolu şirketlerinin kâr marjlarını baskı altında bıraktı.

JetBlue’nun hisse senedi değeri yıl başından bu yana yüzde 42 düştü. Şirket, maliyetleri düşürmek, operasyonel yapısını iyileştirmek ve yolculara yönelik özel hizmetleri genişletmek amacıyla bir program yürütüyor.

JetBlue’nun finansal raporlarına göre, şirketin haziran ayı sonu itibarıyla yaklaşık 1 milyar 660 milyon dolar nakit ve nakit benzeri varlığı bulunurken, toplam borçları ve finansal kiralama yükümlülükleri 8 milyar 500 milyon dolara ulaştı.

JetBlue ve PJT Partners, Reuters’ın haberinin yayımlandığı sırada ajansın yorum talebine yanıt vermemişti.

title: La dialectique peut-elle casser des vitres ?
content:
À l'automne 2010, en plein dans le mouvement des retraites qui secouait alors l'économie et la vie sociale en France, une polémique enflait sur la présence de «

 

casseurs

 

» au sein des manifestations, cristalisée autour de l'affaire du «

 

ninja

 

». Polémique qui n'est que la redite d'un éternel débat

 

; en réalité une approche dogmatique (et gestionnaire) du prolétariat. L'

AG

 Turbin, une assemblée parisienne de plusieurs centaines de personnes, tentait alors d'en expliquer le fond. Il nous a paru intéressant de relire ce texte avant de sombrer, à nouveau, dans des dénonciations malvenues.


Dans le mouvement en cours, la grève se heurte à certaines limites. L'encadrement législatif du «

 

droit de grève

 

» avec les réquisitions qui forcent les grévistes à travailler sous la menace de la prison, le service minimum et l'interdiction des occupations cherchent à limiter les effets de la grève. La légalisation de la part la moins efficace des luttes et la pénalisation de leur part la plus offensive est une des méthodes pour les contrôler - même si le mouvement, quand il est en recherche de puissance et de commun, ne se focalise pas sur ces distinctions et que pour lui la légalité n'est pas une frontière infranchissable ni l'illégalité un but en soi.


Le premier des dispositifs répressifs, c'est le parcours négocié et encadré par les flics, la collaboration des services d'ordre syndicaux et l'attention à ce que tout demeure sous contrôle.


Il en va de même pour la manifestation. Le premier des dispositifs répressifs, c'est le parcours négocié et encadré par les flics, la collaboration des services d'ordre syndicaux et l'attention à ce que tout demeure sous contrôle. Chercher à sortir de ce dispositif, c'est tenter de constituer une force collective, se réapproprier la rue et sortir du simple comptage des forces en présence. C'est ce qui s'est passé le soir du samedi 16 octobre, lorsqu'un groupe de plusieurs centaines de personnes a quitté le rassemblement officiel pour tenter d'occuper l'opéra Bastille dans l'idée d'y tenir une assemblée générale et perturber la retransmission en direct du spectacle. Ce type d'action a eu lieu un peu partout et participait d'une dynamique générale. Ailleurs aussi, on cherchait à sortir du cadre institué des manifestations.


À l'issue de cette tentative, on compte une quarantaine de personnes interpellées et placées en garde à vue. La garde à vue (reconduite automatiquement à 48 heures) est utilisée par les flics comme une punition en tant que telle. Sur ces quarante personnes, huit sont poursuivies, certaines pour participation «

 

à un groupement, même formé de façon temporaire, en vue de la préparation, caractérisée par un ou plusieurs faits matériels, de violences volontaires contre les personnes ou de destructions ou dégradations de biens

 

» et violences sur agents. Parmi les arrêtés se sont aussi trouvés des gens qui étaient déjà sous contrôle judiciaire pour des poursuites liées à des actions antérieures. Leur contrôle leur interdisait de se rencontrer : interpellés tous deux ce soir-là, ils auraient selon la justice violé cette obligation. L'argument ne tient pas : ils ont été arrêtés en compagnie de dizaines de personnes et l'action, appelée publiquement, rassemblait des centaines de personnes. Convoqués par un juge d'instruction, ils ont reçu un avertissement avec menace de réincarcération «

 

la prochaine fois

 

». Cinq des huit qui vont passer en jugement sont aussi placés sous contrôle judiciaire.


Au final, ce qu'on leur reproche, c'est d'avoir participé à une manifestation au lieu de faire profil bas et de rester chez eux. Le contrôle judiciaire est une méthode d'intimidation et d'isolement. Il s'agit d'interdire à certains de fréquenter certains lieux, de voir certaines personnes, d'avoir certaines attitudes : bref il revient à empêcher ceux qui sont dans le collimateur du pouvoir de participer à la contestation sociale sous peine d'emprisonnement. Au total, la répression, comme toujours, se décline en plusieurs versions, s'individualise de manière à briser les solidarités collectives.


Ce qui est juridiquement réprimé dans la participation à cette manifestation, c'est d'avoir été partie prenante d'une action au cours de laquelle quelques vitrines de banque ont été brisées. L'idée, assez bien illustrée par l'usage de cette fameuse «

 

loi sur les bandes

 

» récemment votée, c'est que la simple participation à un rassemblement, un « …

title: Using it/its as pronouns is the reclamation of a slur.
content:
fyshiebusiness

:

oupydogcity

:

lavenderfoxboy-deactivated20240

:

i wish there was more it/its positivity that wasn’t just “hell yeah look at you go funky little goblins/otherwordly beings/freaks/objects”

this is really important actually i wanted to link one of my fav tweets on this subject :>

This is just weird to me because when I hear it/it’s in reference to sapient beings I think of people being treated as objects. People being dehumanized. The past uses of the word for slaves and prisoners who were treated as subhuman.

I’m pretty sure there are very few people who think about it referring to rocks instead of mountains in that context.

People who use it/it’s are allowed to choose that for themselves but I think they should always remember that the word in association with humans specifically comes with baggage.


Using it/its as pronouns is the reclamation of a slur.

And before people go police it: no, this is not a slur that only one specific demographic can reclaim. Any group that’s been unpersoned has at some point been called it. ‘It’ is the universal slur for unpersoning a person.

As usually with the reclamation of a slur, most of the people using it/its are not particularly concerned with being appealing to the majority. They’re doing their own thing, They use the word freaks affectionately for themselves and their friends.

So we can expect “hell yeah look at you go funky little freaks” to be the dominant form of it/its expression for quite a while, until the slur gets so fully reclaimed that people more concerned with respectability start calling themselves it/its and trying to distance themselves from the deliberate freaks and polishing what it/its can mean. OP might be an early participant in that attempt at mainstreaming it/its.

author: Amanda Audi
title: Vorcaro orquestrou venda de bens da Igreja Lagoinha e prometeu expansão de R$ 100 milhões
content:
Uma fungada forte próxima ao microfone para não restarem dúvidas sobre o nível de emoção e uma caprichada na voz embargada: “Ô, Daniel, que o senhor te dê sabedoria, te cubra, te guarde, que ele nos guie e guie você nesse momento a voz de Deus, sempre”. Outra fungada. “É no mundo todo, Dani. É no mundo todo que tá acontecendo, é muito forte, irmão”. E outra fungada. A voz chorosa mineira é do pastor André Valadão, líder da Igreja Lagoinha Global. Essa emoção toda é uma resposta a uma felicitação de aniversário que também faria você chorar.


“Deus me incomodou para uma ação junto contigo. Vou colocar 100mm de reais de doação para abrir novas igrejas”, disse, sem rodeios, ninguém menos que Daniel Vorcaro, então dono do Banco Master e de um sem número de empresas. “Queria que pensasse e orasse e depois me passasse um plano pra implementarmos”, instruiu naquele 16 de abril de 2024.


Depois das prisões de Vorcaro em novembro de 2025 e março de 2026, quando o escândalo Master-BRB já estava em todas as manchetes, Valadão reconheceu que os dois se conhecem há décadas, mas

frisou

 que o relacionamento dos dois se restringia à igreja e não envolvia negócios. Conversas interceptadas pela Polícia Federal (PF) no âmbito da Operação Compliance Zero, às quais a

Agência Pública

 teve acesso, contam outra história.


Em meio a orações, viagens em jatos executivos, convites para Fórmula 1 e declarações de amor (há pelo menos 44 “eu te amo”), os diálogos entre o banqueiro e o pastor revelam uma intrincada rede de influência e a proteção de Vorcaro em círculos de poder evangélicos. Os diálogos entre “Dede” e “Dan Dan”, ou “Dani”, como se chamavam mostram que a relação passava longe de se restringir a doações, mas envolvia também conselhos sobre a gestão dos ativos da Igreja Lagoinha e formas inteligentes de aproveitar o potencial de operações financeiras e imobiliárias na própria rede de igrejas, com especial preocupação em continuar evitando impostos no ecossistema que, segundo Valadão, deve movimentar R$ 1 bilhão até 2030.


As mensagens do WhatsApp do ex-banqueiro mostram uma intensa troca de aconselhamento – espiritual, no caso de Valadão, e financeiro, do lado de Vorcaro. Com muitas citações a Deus e a Jesus, eles faziam articulações com lideranças da direita para viabilizar negócios de interesse comum e contornar crises de imagem – como no

episódio

 em que Vorcaro pediu a intervenção de Valadão para falar com o deputado Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG) após uma postagem que enfureceu o banqueiro. É a pedido de Valadão que Nikolas busca “Dani” para se desculpar e diz que nem teria falado se soubesse que o negócio era dele.


A troca de favores tem duas vias. Em pelo menos dois episódios, Valadão pede ajudas, condicionando o atendimento a se “Deus tocasse no coração” do amigo. Apenas nos eventos de virada de ano da Lagoinha, o toque divino solicitado foi de US$ 350 mil e US$ 450 mil, em 2023 e 2024. Não há registros na mensagens se os gloriosos depósitos chegaram a abençoar as referidas celebrações.


Vende-se e aluga-se


No site vinculado à Igreja da Lagoinha, há 14 imóveis à venda em três municípios mineiros. A avaliação apresentada ao público é de R$ 38,2 milhões no conjunto de prédios comerciais e até fazendas para hospedagem com lazer. O que quem visita o catálogo da Lagoinha desconhece é que a ideia de vender os bens da rede de igrejas partiu do ex-dono do Banco Master.


“Uma das coisas que eu estou pensando é de internacionalizar os bens da Lagoinha toda, sabe? Porque o dinheiro nos EUA, o crédito é muito fácil, né, muito menos juros, né. O juros tá alto hoje, mas ainda assim é baixo. Então seria um ministério sem fins lucrativos,

non for profit

 americano, que detém bens no mundo todo, Europa, África, Brasil, Estados Unidos também, Canadá. Tô fazendo essa mudança, sabe”, conta animadamente André Valadão, em áudio enviado a Vorcaro, que responde:  “Acho excelente ideia”.


 “Como você me aconselhou, eu coloquei vários bens nossos à venda”, continua o pastor. “Tem um pessoal que me procurou também pra gente, tipo, criar um fundo com a quantidade de bens que a gente tem da Lagoinha, sabe? Mas eu acho que, como a maioria deles a gente nem paga imposto, acho que fazer um fundo, coisa assim, podia acabar sendo pior, né? Não sei o que você me aconselha a respeito”, indaga. “Fundo não é vantagem pra você. Legal é fazer base USA e virar global mesmo”, recomenda o empresário, enquanto falam do interesse de acionar advogados “de …

title: Construction Workers' Union, an model for independent unionism
content:
The idea of independent trade unions operating outside the established confederations has long been debated in Turkey. Criticism of existing unions has also led to the establishment of independent organisations in particular sectors.


The debate has been driven by accusations that unions fail to defend workers' rights, cooperate with employers and pay their officials high salaries. Against this backdrop, one union has attracted attention for adopting a different approach.


Founding members killed in massacres


The Construction Workers' Union (Insaat-Is) has distinguished itself through its organising efforts in a sector where trade union activity has historically been limited in Turkey. Operating in the construction industry, which has largely been neglected by trade union confederations, Insaat-Is works in a sector where working conditions make collective bargaining negotiations difficult and maintaining a stable membership has never been possible. Since its official establishment in 2014, the union has become known not only for its trade union struggles but also for its activities in other areas.


The union emerged from discussions and organising efforts prompted by a question raised during a workers' resistance at the Sapphire Tower construction site in 2010: “Why don't construction workers have a union?” The union has also attracted attention for its stance on wider social and political developments. One of its founding members, Ethem Sarısülük, was shot and killed by police in Ankara during the Gezi Resistance.


Six other founding members, Serdar Ben, Tekin Arslan, Erol Ekici, Tayfun Benol, Ismail Kızılçay and Gökmen Dalmaç, were killed in the ISIS attack on a peace rally outside Ankara Train Station on 10 October 2015. The union's history includes several significant workers' struggles in recent years, including the Emaar resistance, the Third Airport resistance and the Financial Centre protests. Insaat-Is has also drawn attention through its solidarity efforts in earthquake-affected regions, as well as statements and campaigns organised during the resistance in Kobanê and Sur.


The union's activities intensified following the Ankara Train Station Massacre. Insaat-Is continued its work with an approach that differed from conventional forms of trade union struggle.


The Construction Workers' Union organising coordinators Anıl Deniz Gider and Yunus Özgür, together with union executive Ekrem Ekşi, spoke to ANF about the union's history, its experiences of struggle and its approach to trade union organising.


 


‘We lost six comrades in Ankara, but we knew we could carry on their work’


Yunus Özgür pointed out that the idea of independent trade unionism emerged at a time when conventional trade union structures had reached their limits. He continued: “The idea of independent trade unionism emerged at a time when the traditional trade union movement in Turkey was no longer sufficient and could no longer respond to the problems and organising needs of the working class.


Why the construction sector? Following the organising efforts of figures such as İsmet Demir in the construction industry during the 1970s and 1980s, neither the Turkish revolutionary movement nor the trade union confederations undertook any significant organising work in this sector. For the confederations, construction is an extremely difficult sector to organise, and the chances of securing a collective bargaining agreement are less than one in a thousand. In other words, there are virtually no membership dues to be collected.”


Özgür explained that the founding idea behind Insaat-Is emerged during the resistance at the Sapphire construction site. He also highlighted the importance of Serdar Ben, one of the union's founding members, who was widely known as Maviş: “The process essentially began with Mustafa's resistance at the Sapphire construction site in 4th Levent. Maviş had a profound influence on both the trade union movement and the revolutionary movement in Turkey. Our comrade Serdar, in particular, pioneered a new path despite the trade union confederations.


Our union representatives who attended the 10 October rally were there not primarily to support a particular peace policy, but to stand alongside the oppressed Kurdish people. We lost six of our representatives there, although calling them representatives feels rather strange. We lost six comrades who had built this union from nothing, who had created it from the ground …

author: Unknown
title: Biçer: Humanitarian and legal steps needed for ill prisoners
content:
Rights violations against sick prisoners continue to increase in prisons. Obstacles to accessing healthcare, delays in hospital transfers and the failure to release seriously ill prisoners are threatening prisoners' right to life.


Sebahat Biçer, an executive of the Federation of Associations for Solidarity with Prisoners' Families (MED TUHAD-FED), spoke to ANF about the rights violations faced by ill prisoners.


‘Urgent steps must be taken regardless of discussions on the peace process’


Sebahat Biçer pointed out that despite ongoing political discussions about the peace process, no concrete progress had been made in prisons. She stressed that releasing sick prisoners was a humanitarian necessity that should not be subject to political bargaining.


Biçer described the lack of progress in prisons and the deep anxiety experienced by prisoners' families: “Yes, that is correct. This peace process has been discussed for more than two years, but so far there has been no progress whatsoever regarding prisons. In fact, regardless of the process, sick prisoners should be released as soon as possible. This is a humanitarian necessity. Yet we have sick prisoners whose coffins could be carried out of prison at any moment. We have prisoners with stage-four cancer. We have sick prisoners who cannot meet their basic needs or sustain their lives independently. Unfortunately, no solution has been found for any of them. Families are deeply worried, and the condition of our friends in prison is deteriorating with each passing day.”


 


‘Even those who have completed their sentences are held hostage and threatened’


Sebahat Biçer said prisoners whose health was deteriorating were being subjected to pressure by prison administrations, including those who had completed their sentences but had not been released.


Biçer said: “Take Önder Poyraz, for example. He uses a wheelchair and cannot meet any of his basic needs, including bathing. His fellow prisoners take care of his needs, yet he is still being held in prison. Similarly, nothing is being done even for seriously ill prisoners who have completed 30 years in prison and should have been released. Although they have served their sentences, they are not being released.


We have prisoners with stage-four cancer who are approaching the end of their lives. They should be spending their final days with their families, but instead they are being held hostage in prison. Looking at the current process, unfortunately, no measures have been taken to address either their situation or that of prisoners whose releases have been postponed. They are being held entirely at the discretion of prison administrations. They are now being threatened with statements such as, ‘We will keep you here until the very end. You will leave in a coffin.’ Our friends are being held hostage under increasingly severe conditions of isolation, accompanied by such threats.”


‘They are beaten on their way to treatment, and violations are covered up’


Biçer described the conduct of prison officials and incidents of physical violence against prisoners being taken for medical treatment.


She said: “As I mentioned, prison administrations and even guards make threats, saying things like, ‘We will always prevent your release.’ One of these sick prisoners is Devrim Ayık. He has a colon condition and is completely blind in one eye. Even with glasses, he can only see up to one metre ahead with his other eye. He is beaten while being taken for medical treatment and severely beaten again on his return to prison. Attempts are being made to cover up what happened. His family noticed his condition during a prison visit and began pursuing the matter. Many others are being subjected to similar treatment.


Recently, our friend Celal Yıldırım in Urfa also suffered a heart attack, and his condition is deteriorating with each passing day. Yet they are deliberately keeping these prisoners behind bars. They are not being released for political reasons. Our friends are being detained even though they have completed their sentences.


We will not abandon this struggle. We will stand by our friends until the very end and be their voice outside prison. We will also continue to stand alongside their families.”


‘There are nearly 400 ill prisoners, 180 of them seriously ill’


Sebahat Biçer provided figures on the overall situation in prisons, criticised the authorities' indifference and called on the state to take concrete action. Biçer …

author: Unknown
title: Mihemed: We will continue our struggle for constitutional recognition of Kurdish in Syria
content:
Reactions continue in Rojava Kurdistan to the Damascus transitional government's decision concerning the Kurdish language. On 17 October 2026, the Initiative for the Constitutional Recognition of Kurdish and Its Adoption as an Official Language in Syria was announced in Qamishlo. Hesen Mihemed, a member of the initiative, spoke about its activities, aims and objectives.


Hesen Mihemed said there was an urgent need for such an initiative today. He said, “We worked to establish this initiative because our aim was to secure official status for our language. For the past 15 years, students in Rojava have generally been reading, writing and receiving their education in Kurdish, their mother tongue. Unfortunately, under the latest decision, the Syrian Minister of Education has allocated only a few hours, three hours in total, to Kurdish. Even if some other subjects, such as philosophy, mathematics and history, can also be taught in Kurdish, this is unfortunately not enough.


The Kurdish people are an indigenous people, as stated in Article 13 of the Syrian presidential decree. Kurds have rights as Syrian citizens. They must be able to speak, read and receive education in their own language. Unfortunately, however, there has recently been a retreat from these rights. That is why our initiative seeks recognition of Kurdish as an indigenous language alongside Arabic and aims to secure its official status. Just as Arabs can study and receive education in their own language, Kurds must also be able to receive education in theirs. This is why we considered it important to establish such an initiative.”


‘Efforts to secure official status for Kurdish will continue’


Hesen Mihemed stressed that efforts to secure official recognition of Kurdish would continue. Mihemed said: “Kurdish must be permanently recognised as an official language in Syria's future constitution. We will carry out our work towards this goal. They acknowledge that Kurdish is an indigenous language and that Kurds are Syrian citizens. But if the rights verbally acknowledged for Kurds are not reflected in practice and enshrined in the constitution, it cannot truly be said that those rights have been recognised. In such circumstances, there can be no genuine justice regarding Kurdish rights. That is why we are making these efforts. There are human rights organisations, civil society organisations and institutions such as the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF). There are organisations that defend the right of every people to speak and receive education in their own language, particularly when it comes to children's education.


We believe that if we continue our efforts, maintain our activities and pursue our work with determination, we can secure our rights. We will establish relations with legal organisations, international institutions and all organisations working on children's rights and issues concerning children. We will also maintain contact with national institutions working in education and language teaching, as well as civil society organisations, intellectuals and individuals concerned with the rights of peoples. Our aim is to establish relations with every organisation working on language rights. We have already established contacts with international and civil society organisations both inside and outside Syria. We contacted and visited them before formally establishing and launching the initiative. We met with representatives of Assyrians, Armenians, Chaldeans and other communities. We developed relations with individuals and institutions representing different peoples.


We explained that we are a civil initiative, that we are not affiliated with any political party and that our work is peaceful. Our objective is to ensure that Kurdish is permanently recognised as an official language in Syria's future constitution. We do not want division. Demanding official status for one language does not mean diminishing or eliminating another language, nor does it mean dividing the country. On the contrary, it represents richness and diversity. In many countries around the world, education is provided in two, three, four or even five languages. We want this to be possible in our own country as well. We are asking for support in this regard. The people we met told us that they supported us, that they could join the initiative and that Kurds were entitled to this right …

author: Unknown
title: Sevda Karaca: War policies undermine unity and labour struggles - Part One
content:
Sevda Karaca, Deputy Chair of the Labour Party (EMEP) and MP for Antep, answered ANF's questions about labour struggles and the struggle for peace.


Karaca said, “War permeates every aspect of social life. Workers' demands for higher wages, the right to strike, women's struggle for equality and people's democratic demands can suddenly be pushed into the background by debates over 'national security', 'the survival of the state' or the 'domestic front'. The racism, nationalism and chauvinism being fuelled also prevent people, women and young people from coming together around shared demands.”


Karaca stressed that Turkish workers also had a responsibility to oppose the policies of their own ruling classes and support the Kurdish people's demands for peace, equality and democracy. She added, “This is necessary not only as an act of solidarity but also to defend the independent interests of their own class. Because in an environment where peoples are turned against one another, it becomes harder to develop a common struggle against capital.”


How do you assess the current state of the labour struggle in Turkey? Is it sufficient, and where does it fall short?


One of the greatest contradictions in Turkey's labour struggle is this: workers' anger is growing, working and living conditions are deteriorating, and individual pockets of resistance are continuing and spreading. Yet this accumulation of struggle has not developed into an effective nationwide class movement or an independent political force representing the working class.


Workers in textiles, metalworking, logistics, mining and the service sector are engaged in fierce struggles over wages, working conditions and trade union rights across industrial regions with very different characteristics throughout the country. They continue to resist despite the threat of dismissal, pressure from employers, obstacles to trade union organising and the corruption of the trade union bureaucracy.


These struggles show us that the working class has not surrendered. However, the experience gained in one factory or one struggle is not being carried over sufficiently to other workplaces, sectors and cities. Resistance often remains confined to individual workplaces and struggles to develop into a collective class consciousness and political force.


What do you attribute these difficulties to?


We cannot attribute these shortcomings to a lack of willingness among workers to struggle. The limitations imposed by trade union bureaucracy, the lack of organisation, fear of unemployment, increasingly precarious employment and political repression are significant obstacles. But socialists and labour organisations must also confront their own responsibilities. Exposing workers' problems and voicing their legitimate demands is not enough. We must establish connections between these problems, bring struggles together, help workers develop confidence in their own strength and link economic demands to a political programme.


The connection between economic and political struggle does not emerge automatically. What we need today is to unite the fragmented experiences of the working class around a common struggle. We must ensure that workers have a say not only in confronting the employers in their own factories, but also in challenging the economic and political system that determines their working and living conditions. The working class needs to organise itself as a force capable of shaping society as a whole. We need to develop a strategy of struggle that transforms workers' scattered anger into collective strength, builds political action out of everyday experiences and enables the working class to shape society according to its own demands and objectives.


Are socialists sufficiently self-critical? Is enough thought being given to why poorer sections of society turn to ruling parties?


The government does not merely control economic resources and the institutions of the state. It also intervenes in people's everyday lives, their sense of belonging, their expectations and their relationships of trust. It creates the everyday, consistent and long-term mechanisms needed to sustain this influence. We cannot explain the political choices of a worker or a poor family solely in terms of economic interests.


People also make political choices based on belonging, trust, identity, solidarity and expectations for the future. Through the networks of everyday relationships it has …

title: Hawari: Syria could lose a century without guaranteed rights
content:
The transitional administration established in Syria following the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad's government faces fundamental challenges, including political legitimacy, economic recovery and the protection of the rights of the country's diverse communities. Journalist and writer Nidal Hawari spoke to ANF about a range of issues, from tensions in Hasakah (Hesekê) and the situation of Alawites and Druze to regional power struggles and strategic straits. He warned that the administration's failure to develop lasting solutions to these problems was increasing uncertainty and deepening social tensions.


Hawari stressed that developments in Syria could not be considered in isolation from one another.


‘The legitimacy of the transitional administration is disputed’


Hawari pointed to the structure of Syria's transitional administration, saying that the current political order had not been established by a government directly elected by the people. He said the way the administration had been formed, from the presidency to the transitional institutions, had raised questions about its legitimacy. He added that the structure established under the leadership of Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) was not based on a consensus encompassing all communities in the country.


Hawari said that the forces which had gained influence in Syria following the overthrow of the Assad government were attempting to reorganise their political and regional interests, but had failed to establish a common political position even among themselves. He pointed out that the administration had been unable to stabilise the country politically, economically or legally, placing the process of rebuilding state institutions at risk. Hawari stressed that a transition to a democratic system required the establishment of accountable institutions based on the will of the people and subject to public oversight.


‘The economic crisis is deepening and artificial crises are being created’


Hawari warned that Syria was facing a severe economic crisis, pointing to difficulties in paying public employees' salaries and the administration's dependence on external resources, which restricted its ability to act independently. He said uncertainty surrounding future support from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and other countries was increasing the pressure on the administration. Any reduction or suspension of foreign assistance would make it even more difficult for the authorities to maintain public services.


Hawari stressed that the economic crisis could not be separated from the political crisis. He said the administration's failure to resolve economic problems was intensifying social tensions and creating conditions conducive to new political crises and security problems.


He also expressed the view that artificial crises and hostilities were being created between different sections of society to conceal economic problems. Hawari said this was placing additional pressure on communities outside the central administration or those demanding recognition of their identities and rights.


‘Tensions in Hasakah and the provocation of tribes are not independent of external factors’


Hawari addressed attacks against Kurds in Hasakah and the positions adopted by Arab tribes. He said these developments could not be reduced solely to relations between the transitional administration and the Kurds, stressing the need to examine the political positions of the tribes and the regional influences shaping them. He pointed out that Arab tribes held differing positions among themselves. Some had previously issued statements supporting the agreement between the Kurds and the transitional government within the framework of integration, but had subsequently retreated from those positions.


Hawari stressed that this shift was significant in the context of regional power struggles. He suggested that the conflict of interests between Turkey and Israel could also influence the positions of local actors, pointing to the incitement of certain Arab tribes against the Kurds. He linked the continuation of attacks and tensions, despite the flexibility shown and concessions made by the Kurds on certain issues during the integration process, to the absence of a lasting legal framework in Syria and interference by certain states. Hawari stressed that lasting peace in Syria could not be achieved solely through temporary agreements between local actors.
